BUNDLE 76 b

(from the notebooks of the first Secretaries)

Conferences

1870 – 71 – 72

Given in the House of Piacenza on the evening of 24 April 1870

On the mutual love that the Daughters of Saint Anne must have among themselves

The conference of today, it seems to me, I announced to you would be on the mutual love that the Daughters of Saint Anne must have among themselves. Before speaking to you of this, however, the Father gave me, by obedience, to tell you a few more words on the chapter of your Holy Rules which says how you must go along the street. Truly it grieves me to have to repeat to you what the Father told you so many times, and far better than I, since I am not capable enough of explaining this to you. That is, that you must never stop in the street with anyone.

If it should happen that someone had to speak to you or give you something, for example a note, a letter, etc., you must modestly, and always continuing on your way, answer him: Come to the house, and there you will be satisfied in everything. And if any one of you, not being from Piacenza, should lose her way to the house of the sick person, that is, the street that leads to it, or should wish to know the address of the dwelling of some sick person, let her always ask a poor woman, that is, always persons who are poorer, and never gentlemen and ladies.

I tell you again, you must go with your eyes modestly lowered, but not, however, in such a way that you do not see where you are going.

The Daughter of Saint Anne in the street must be, by her bearing and modesty, the good example to all the world. And what do you expect worldly people, who live on appearances alone, to say on seeing a Daughter of Saint Anne standing still in the street, talking now with one, now with another, or else turning her eyes here and there, prying now into one thing, now into another? Yes, my dear ones, you who as nurses spend your life more outside than inside the house must of necessity be more on guard over yourselves, and think that the eyes of all the world rest upon you: fix it well in your minds that on this point depends the honour of your house and of your newborn Institute. But enough on this; it seems to me that I have told you enough, not to speak of the Father; it is now for you to put it into practice.

We shall now take up again our conference on the love that you must bear one another, which unfortunately until now I have not yet been able to see in you as I should wish: all of one heart, seeking mutually to help one another, indeed proud to be able to do a kindness to a sister, seeking to find out what the other desires in order to procure it for her, sharing in her sorrows, in her troubles; in short, to be of one mind, one heart. This is what I should wish from you; and yet this happiness I have not yet been able to have: one flees from the other, you speak to one another with little charity, etc., etc. So too at recreation I should like to see you all united; it seems that you are there by force and for fear of being punished, deprived of Communion, and one waits for nothing but the sound of the bell, which by force brings us together, to receive the obedience and then go to one’s office; and there, with those sisters one is with, then one laughs, one talks of this one and that one, of the things that have happened in the house. And so what is done? The Rules are neglected, faults are committed upon faults, sins upon sins; the time that is appointed for mitigated silence is made to serve for recreation, and then one goes to Holy Communion. Ah! My dear Sisters, and what is it that we are doing? What Communions are these? How can you recollect yourselves? And so what is done? One makes that little thanksgiving, if indeed it is made, distracted; one approaches Communion without even thinking of it, and in such a way one makes the thanksgiving. In this moment so fortunate not a thought is found for one’s Jesus, and with a distracted mind one makes that little thanksgiving. And then they complain that they do not feel the love of the Lord. Ah! How do you expect the Lord to make His voice, His caresses felt by a heart, by a soul which He finds absent from itself? You will not attain that holy and sweet union with the Lord in which I should so much like to see you, until you are more recollected during the day and observe, as the Holy Rule says, mitigated silence.

Returning to speak of recreation, I tell you, as I have already told you so many times: let one speak of one point of the Rules, another of another; one never knows, even the most ignorant may in that moment be given by God some light more than another, and may say some word to someone, some good sentiment that may serve her for her spirit; and thus you would profit one another, doing as was done a year ago when I too was able to be with you at recreation.

If one has some little thing to laugh about, let her keep it for recreation, but let it not be one of those foolish things. For, my God, what I heard the other day! I assure you my blood ran cold on hearing them.

You will say to me: But… Mother, you too took part and laughed with us… Yes, dear daughters, I laughed and questioned you, but do you know why? To enter into your heart, to uncover your faults at the root… But Mother, now you are revealing yourself… Yes, I will tell you, I am obliged to it in conscience; I must do it in order to see how far you go. So the other day, after the whole of recreation had been spent in silence, as soon as the bell for work had rung, behold, recreation was being held in the laundry; I happened by chance to be in a place where I heard all that was being said and laughed at. I said within myself: My God, see what these creatures are doing! Truly I was seething as I listened to you, and I wanted to come and make you stop; then I thought: let us let them be, I shall speak to them of it. And so mitigated silence has not yet been obtained; one goes about all day with the stocking in hand, looking out of the window to see who is coming, who is leaving, what the Superiors are doing, what they are saying…

So too, when the Superior gives the signal in the morning after the thanksgiving, you must all leave the Church and go at once to breakfast all together, and not do as is done, one now, one later, so that those who leave the Church after the others, out of embarrassment at going to ask for breakfast, would rather stay fasting; and thus of one sin they make two. And here a remedy was applied to these things, so that, by the grace of the Lord, it was no longer committed [?], and all in a body go down to breakfast, and likewise to dinner and to the offices.

On various points of the Holy Rules

given in Piacenza on the evening of 19-6-70

This evening the Mother spoke to us on various points of the Rule in which she finds us wanting, namely, not being prompt in rising in the morning, nor exact at the bell for Meditation; and she told us that by failing on this point it is impossible for us to fulfil exactly the duties proper to the day.

My daughters, she said to us, if you knew what sorrow I feel on seeing that the thanksgiving for the night is begun thus with so few, you would certainly not do it. Meditation is the pivot of all our works, because there the resolutions for the day are made, which then at the evening examination one considers whether they have been carried out. By failing on this point one multiplies sins upon venial sins, and one comes to commit mortal ones. I have also noticed that strict silence is broken.

She told us to study Chapter 11 of the Rules, to learn it by heart, for if we managed to practise it we would find in it all perfection. Already, she said, you have experienced that the Holy Mother does not wish even the least point of the Rule to be transgressed. Yes, although we try to keep our faults hidden, sooner or later they are discovered. Oh! what displeasure the Holy Mother felt at the last Chapter, in which, out of human respect or fear of being sent away, you hid various faults. I can tell you that instead of serving for your sanctification it served to burden your conscience all the more. This Chapter serves you as an amusement, and it has been reduced to what? With sorrow I must say it: to an irreverence, to kissing the ground.

Do not think that I know these things by extraordinary means, no, no, nor by imagination, but by a most ordinary, most material and most positive means. For charity’s sake, my dear daughters, I recommend to you holy modesty, a virtue so delicate, and of which to my sorrow I see you make little account and esteem. Do you perhaps think that your eyes do not see? To this point, I know for certain, you have not arrived, for I can tell you I studied it for so many years and saw by experience how difficult it is to look without seeing. To know whether we truly have this virtue we must be jealous of ourselves. It will never be a want of modesty if, beyond the hand, two fingers’ breadth of the arm are seen, but near the elbow, yes. Well, of this I know you make really little account, because I know from the sick that you pull your veil up too much, that you put the kerchief round your neck, and likewise unfasten your collar; these are acts contrary to this virtue. So too I recommend to you nurses to keep yourselves clean, to wash your hands, even every moment if need be, to be gracious with the sick, for I learned of things that greatly displeased the Holy Mother. So too I recommend that you taste the broth, prepare it before midnight, provide for the needs of the sick person, and above all not separate from one another for any need whatever, because if this should happen, she would immediately be sent away from the Institute.

I say this because I know that the Father too insists on this point, and since the will of my Superior is also mine, so what pleases him is also my desire; if I could foresee his desires, I would most willingly carry them out.

Now today I would advise you, as I advised in the other House, with which I was well pleased, and as I shall advise in all the houses, to take on the day of retreat, as your examination for the whole month, one chapter of the Rules, beginning with the first, and to endeavour to observe it, and every day at the midday examination to see whether it has been observed, and at the end of the month to give an exact account of it to the Father or to the Superior. In this way the Holy Rules are learned without your even noticing it, and what is more, you would find yourselves practising them with exactness, without effort; you would grow in vocation and persevere to the end of your days, and one day in Paradise we shall enjoy together the fruits of our labour.

On silence, given at Piacenza

On the evening of 10 October 1870

When the evening recreation was over, since, it being Sunday, there was no work, all of us seated around our dear Mother in the room appointed for recreation begged her to tell us something about our Holy Rules. She willingly consented and began to speak on Silence and on the habit of virtue that a Religious, a Daughter of Saint Anne, must put on, and she began in this way.

What must I tell you this evening about silence? That little account is made of it, it is not observed at all, nor exactly; this Rule is a most important point for a religious.

In silence everything is contained; it is the principal foundation of every virtue, and that is why the Saints weighed it much [?] and so are always on guard to observe it. I should also like the religious, before putting on the habit, to clothe her heart too; and with what garment? With the garment of the virtues; for what would it matter that she has one garment rather than another, that she puts on the holy habit of a religious, and then always has her heart attached to worldly things, that she still keeps all her worldly affections and habits? It is not the habit, no, that makes a good religious, but rather the heart, that this be empty of every affection, of every attachment to her own will, so that, free and unbound, it may freely fly away to its God, who is the centre of its affections and is its all. Yes, I know well, expressly to keep us humble, so that we may have recourse to Him with greater confidence.

Yes, it pleases Jesus that we do such violence to the Heart of the Lord when, repentant of our faults, we cast ourselves at His feet, ask His pardon for them and beg grace not to fall into them again, that He cannot help hearing us at once and strengthening us. He said one day to Saint Gertrude: It pleases me so much when you come all humble and, acknowledging your misery, ask my pardon. Before putting on the habit we must give our heart a good washing, empty it of the things of the earth and clothe it, that is, always nourish good desires of overcoming ourselves, of ridding ourselves now of one vice, now of another; one day to set about it with earnestness, another day to observe another, and so on and on, if we truly wish to become saints. That saint who sanctified himself without penances, what did he ever do? He was most exact in observing the Rules, even the very least, and he had his heart truly clothed with the religious habit that he wore.

Oh! if every morning, in putting on this Sacred habit, we clothed our heart as religious!

So too with prayer: it is not fitting to pray much, to say many Rosaries, many Paters, many Aves in haste, without knowing what one is saying, but to pray with the heart, if we wish to have a grace, to be heard in what we ask. Oh! then how Jesus would hear us! Let us say it to Jesus many times, until He grants it to us; and if He does not hear us, does not grant us at once what we ask, He does it expressly to see our constancy, our humility in asking it of Him. How many saints have prayed and asked for the same grace for years, for continuous years!

A Saint Monica prayed 14 years for the conversion of Saint Augustine. So let us not think that we can overcome a vice in ourselves in a moment. Saint Francis de Sales took more than twelve years to rid himself of one.

For example, one has the vice of telling lies; well then, today she refrains and tells one or two fewer, tomorrow she does the same, and doing so every day she will come to the end of the year and find in her Examination that she has told a good portion fewer than the year before; and so, little by little, without much effort, she will find herself entirely free of this vice. So the Saints did, and so must we do too, if we truly wish to sanctify ourselves.

God, when He sees that one of His servants truly wishes to perfect herself, gives her a strong arm to lean upon. Let us say our prayers with attention and with fervour, and we shall obtain everything.

How the observance of the Holy Rules

Is a principal means of acquiring

the love of God

In the observance of the Holy Rules we have the means of acquiring the love of God, for without a lively desire to observe them exactly I could never attain to it. If we neither have nor nourish this lively desire, there is thereafter formed a barrier wall against the love of God, and once this is raised, we shall do nothing good. I ask myself: what would one do for a person one loves? What would one not do? Everything; even if it cost us pains and sacrifices of every kind, one feels nothing, one would suffer everything, provided we could give pleasure to that person. And if this person gave us a book and told us to observe what is written in it, at once we would set about observing with earnestness what it contains, in order to content that person. And to please God, what shall we do? I hear the Holy Mother answering: the observance of the Holy Rules. These contain every sort of mortification, that sweet fragrance which so pleases God, which gives Him so much delight, and they can bring us to the highest sanctity; but we must desire, and make every effort, to observe them all, even the very least, which seem nothing to us, for these serve as a help to observe the other great ones. So, going along the street, to observe that beautiful rule which says: You shall go along the street in silence, modestly; instead, how many times we fail; for example, the companion says a word, the other, thinking it a small thing, answers her; so one word leads to another and it ends in laughter. Suppose that at that moment a person passes by: this person hears, takes notice, and behold, is scandalised, because a religious person, and especially a Daughter of Saint Anne, must be by her grave bearing the admiration, the good example of the Cities. On the contrary, by doing as I said above, the Institute loses by it, because, you see, a single word is enough; and above all, behold our Holy Rule neglected, which is the worst of all evils.

So too, when going to bed, to observe silence as our Holy Rule says: from after the Rosary until the Mass of the following day, thinking of the point of Meditation that one has heard and that one will have to meditate in the morning. So too, on waking, to think that within those sacred walls where we live dwells our Bridegroom, that divine Love who is watching us and who awaits nothing else from us but our love.

My dear ones, when we find it burdensome to do something commanded by obedience, or a rule is repugnant to our senses, let us not be dismayed; this does not matter, the feeling, the experiencing of this resentment; it is enough that we do it with patience; indeed, it is then that we relieve our Jesus on the Cross.

The Superior: to obey her promptly. When it seems to us that she scolds us wrongly and we feel our self-love rising up, see what happens: it is because we do not look upon our Superior as if we saw Jesus, as if it were He Himself who speaks to us, who commands us. Ah! If we nourished this true faith of seeing Jesus in our Superior, how we would run with humility to hear the admonitions, with what reverence we would stand before her, and run with humility to tell her all our failings so as to amend them. I know that our good Jesus is all charity, is ready to forgive us, to help us; but this He does when He sees that we have a firm and good will to amend and that we fall through inadvertence; but He is equally a judge, and therefore most severe, when He sees that we do it on purpose. So too, when we pray, let us pray with perseverance, let us not lose heart on seeing that we are not heard at once. Eh! Dear daughters, at times how much Jesus wishes to be prayed to, in order to see our humility and perseverance. There was, you see, and not so long ago, a good soul who was always asking the Lord for a grace and could never obtain it, and to obtain it she asked for it after Communion; one day the Lord answered her: Eh! My dear one, know that before having what you ask of me you have to suffer, and suffer much. And do you think you will obtain at once the grace you want without any effort? Without suffering anything, for that Jesus who comes to you with His wounds open, and to His beloved brides, to find refreshment? And by whom does Jesus wish to be tended, if not by His beloved Brides, by those who observe the Holy Rules well? He says to them: Look at me, see these open wounds, relieve me! And instead He finds them hard!… what sorrow He then feels! To whom shall we turn if not to the Eternal Father, for you know well what delight He feels when we offer Him the Wounds of His Divine Son; and the more we observe them, the more this divine fire will go on growing in us, and we shall be sure that by observing these we can have all the graces we desire. We have seen Blessed Bergmans, who became a saint, and in what way? By the observance of the Holy Rules alone. I shall not keep to ascetical theory [?], for we might come to great discussions, but I shall keep to the shortest way, which will lead you to Holiness; yes, it is the road of the observance of the Holy Rules. And indeed I keep saying within myself: what will become of me, my God, who am continually in the Parlour, I who fail in the prayers of the Community? I assure you that I feel real sorrow over it, but I do everything for the good of our poor House, so as always to dispatch the affairs of this Institute, to be able to go forward, to grow great, and to leave you well established.

On obedience, given at Sampierdarena

on 6.11.1870

Obedience is the shortest way to make us saints. Once a devout person asked a Saint what the Lord wanted of her. Obey the one who is at the back of the Church (he was her Confessor) and you will become a saint.

Obedience is a kind of authority that one has over others.

The masters of the Spirit make use of it when they have in their care a soul who is on the way of perfection, and she becomes aware of it, having a kind of communicativeness [?]. Obedience, it is commonly said, is that way which leads to the Royal Palace of Paradise; the person who obeys knows for certain that she does not mistake, that she never errs, whatever the thing she does by obedience, which is commanded her. There is at times one who says: There, because I obeyed I find myself in a muddle, my spirit is upside down; what do you think? Are these signs of a soul who wishes to keep to a way of perfection, who wishes to go to Paradise? To me it seems quite the contrary. Yes, my daughters, obedience is what makes us go to Paradise; but such a one will say: I have a cantankerous Superior, who makes me lose patience with her uncivil manners. I shall answer her: Have you a Superior who makes you deviate from your Rules? No; but she is cantankerous, she does not know how to adapt her spirit to my character, she commands me with little charity, with arrogance, things that I cannot do. Even if there were a Superior who made you deviate from your rules, who commanded you things contrary to them, even here you must obey and then report to whom you ought, because whoever obeys, whoever makes himself a slave of another’s will, will never fail (it is understood, in things that do not lead to sin), but will gain great merits before God and will be saved, because it is known for certain that by obeying one is saved; and whoever does not obey, who wishes to be led, guided by his own will, will hardly be saved, because, guided by his own caprice, little by little he will find himself engulfed in an abyss, in a labyrinth of evils, from which with difficulty, and I would almost say impossibly, he will come out. Our heart is made for God; God alone is its Master; it loves God; before knowing Him it already feels the beating of His divine love; but this is not enough, we must love Him with something more. Saint Philip Neri used to say: Give me two fingers’ breadth of your forehead and you will become a saint. We must let ourselves be guided in everything and for everything by the one who holds for you the place of God on this earth, manifesting our spirit to him, and then live, remain at peace in what he will do or tell us. There are certain souls who love penances, but of those… you understand me, the ones they themselves want, who then say: I have a Confessor who will hear nothing of penances nor of spirit; shall I do well to do as he tells me? Shall I sanctify myself? God will keep the obedient one thus as long as He wills; when He has designed other ways for this person, perhaps higher ones, He will know well how to open the road to him and make of him, lead him as He wills; it is enough that that soul be obedient. God does not lead her by other roads; and indeed I can assure you that I have had to do with many souls who were never content with anything; the Confessor did not suit them [?]; and so what happens? That in the end they become simple-minded, they lose their heads; and these are called persons who do not wish to do the will of God, but rather their own.

I cannot understand how a soul who obeys can be upset, for whatever may happen to her she will always be at peace, being always able to say: I have obeyed. A person who is desirous of obeying does everything well; she remembers her holy Rules, she remembers poverty, which is the jewel of the saints. She remembers modesty, she remembers her Rules, because by obeying them, by observing them, she obeys God, her Superiors, who are means to sanctify her. Obedience teaches me that I must be silent at such a time, observe strict silence, mitigated silence, speak only of the things of God; obedience teaches me to leave everything at the voice of the Superior or at the sound of the bell; how many things come to us in the day to obey! In the morning we ought to say: I wish to be the mirror of my body [?], I wish to be a good soldier for my soul. If we reflected on what this body serves for: when our body obeys, when it has received those reproofs, our body puts itself under a machine and works like the mill. In the morning, as soon as we have risen, we have the occasion to sanctify our body: the waking call is heard, the body would like to sleep two minutes more, that quarter of an hour, and one says: I shall wait for the bell, and one dozes on until the bell rings; then one wakes and dresses with eyes closed, to enjoy a little more of that pleasure. Doing so, by dint of softness, which leaves the soul bereft of every grace, I go into the Church, and there what do I do? I sprawl on the bench to make the meditation and I fall asleep there, and I sleep until the signal for the meditation wakes me. This renders the soul incapable of receiving any light from God, and the poor thing, little by little deprived of what should sustain her, that is, of the lights of the inspirations that God in this time of meditation [?], grows weak and dies. But if, on the contrary, there is that soldier who says: Ah, you donkey of a body, you have slept enough! And as soon as awake gives a thought to God: Lord, she says to Him, today I wish to be obedient in everything. My Jesus, I promise You to wish to obey the least sign of my Superior; and then to keep, to be constant in the promise she has made. Ah! a Bishop said to me one day: Rosa, when a promise is made to God, it is not to a man that it is made, and therefore it must be kept, and one must think well before making it, for we do not promise to a man but to God. And tell me, are we not able to keep a promise for one day, are we not able? For example: in the morning the Superior finds she has to reprove us for something; and are we not able to go and cast ourselves at her feet and ask her pardon? Ah! How beautiful obedience is; if we spoke of it, we should have to stay until night relishing it.

I have obeyed the least of my fellow sisters: she calls me to help her for a moment; here I am, ready; the Rules tell me that for a quarter of an hour I may do it; here I am, ready. Saint Aloysius and Saint Francis de Sales had taken, besides the other virtues, obedience to practise in a special way. Saint Francis de Sales obeyed his servant, Saint Aloysius the Lay Brothers, because they knew that obedience to inferiors was of greater merit before God, and that one acquires the whole merit of obedience.

Benefits that obedience brings

given at Sampierdarena

on the evening of 10 December 1870

Obedience, we know it as a maxim, is the virtue that forms the saints. It is useless to put into one’s head: I fulfil my duty, but I feel that I must direct myself in the manner of doing penances, mortifications; but I do not know; the Superior always commands me things that seem to me little suited to my spirit. I feel within me that I want to become a saint in my own way. I ask whether, thinking thus, I am practising obedience, and whether, in short, I am fulfilling my obligation in the state in which God has placed me.

We have never heard that the women saints judged for themselves, and I say to my God: and why? Because they knew that the virtue of obedience was what made them saints. At once all those who truly wished to become saints, like Saint Augustine, gave themselves to the virtue of obedience. The person who intends to obey does not wish to judge for herself, for if she did so she would be a hypocrite, and she could be certain that all her works would serve to give pleasure to the enemy. Let us place our will in the hands of our Superiors; let us do as many do, who say: let my Superiors do with me what they will. But certain persons, after having said this, when we come to practice, to deeds, what does one hear said? But I… cannot… impossible… it would be much better to do this business or that other, which would be more to my liking. For example: tomorrow there is adoration; I would gladly go and remain a little before the Lord and make an hour of adoration; but the Superior says no, and in fact I have not been in church: this is true obedience. Tomorrow there is a nurse who is little to my liking and falls to me as companion; she does not understand, knows nothing of the sick, has little grace, etc. I will tell you the reason is this: the Lord, to make you perform an act of virtue, to exercise you in obedience, has given her to you expressly as a companion. What must that soul say? She must exclaim: Dear Jesus, it will never be as much suffering as You had to suffer going to Calvary in the midst of the Jews, followed by people who vied with one another as to who could most torment You, ill-treat You, calumniate You, and in short make You suffer. On the contrary, I with this person have not so much to bear as You, who have borne with me after so many sins, so many betrayals that I have done You. I will try to use good manners with this companion, I will take care of her, I will try to set her on the good path of virtue. Behold an heroic act; you have made an act of perfection, you have gained a place for Heaven. I hear that the Superior reproves me many times; it may be the case that I am innocent; what shall I say? I will humble myself at her feet, saying within me: dear Jesus, I thank You, You have given me a sorbet, You have given me a sweet for my soul.

Now tell me, instead of doing this, what is done? Excuses upon excuses; one wants to have one’s say to the very last; one would claim to make the Superior be silent; and is this wishing to become saints? Keeping to a way of perfection? Ah! Certainly not! You may well say: by doing in this way I lose my Soul, and I lose it because I will to; because, I answer you, you want to keep the crest of pride held high. The Mother has to be absent; she leaves word of something to be done, she leaves an order; obedience tells me to carry it out promptly. So must the Portress do. The superior leaves word: you shall not take lights outside the appointed hour; and instead one sees nothing but lights lit on every side: is this the obedience which, you say, you mean to practise? Ah! A truly shameful thing! I swallow pills of wormwood every moment. I tell the truth: it is a painful thing for me to have to carry out the voice of command, instead of your hearing the voice of Jesus with sweetness.

So too this blessed poverty: to endeavour to put this vow into practice. Truly it is enough to make one weep to see that so little account is made of it; things are wasted uselessly; it is a thing that truly makes one shudder, to think that we live on providence.

I always see that our good Jesus maintains us every day with the treasure of Heaven, wherefore all the more must one endeavour not to waste things, for these are the goods of the poor. One must think that this little economy which is made, now on one thing, now on another, every day, at the end of the year can maintain that place for the girl in danger, open the door to a poor Postulant who perhaps will have a well-founded vocation but, being poor, cannot enter any Religious Order; to endeavour, by saving a centesimo on one thing, now on another, and so one comes, without noticing it, to make some small sum; and behold, from it we could withdraw from sin so many young girls who find themselves in the middle of the street, abandoned by all, in danger of losing their innocence, and give them back to God. I keep saying to Jesus: for charity’s sake, Jesus, do not punish us, show us mercy; all day my prayers are: Jesus, keep us under the powerful hand of Your mercy, have pity on us. When I think, my daughters, that in so many houses they do not know how to live, and we, my God, one hundred and twenty persons: only the sack of the mercy and providence of God maintains us!

We, by obeying, by endeavouring to put poverty into practice, how many things we could save, and so give some relief to the house. In truth the Vow of Poverty is not put into practice at all; one must ask the Superior’s permission in anything whatever, as our Holy Rules say; not take this thing or that other without permission. Oh! how beautiful submission is! My daughters, blessed are you if you know its worth! How happy I shall be if one day I have the fortune of putting obedience into practice! In truth, I would unstitch my apron so as to run at once to the Superior for that needleful of thread that would be needed to sew it, and say to the Superior: do you permit this needleful? How beautiful this Vow is: to be master of nothing; this is the Vow of a religious: we have everything and we have nothing; this is the grace that God gives to that soul in calling her to Religious life.

Whoever puts into practice the virtue of obedience is sure to set foot in Paradise, ascending to it by a royal road such as that of obedience, and to enjoy her Jesus for an eternity.

Whether the Superior be a simpleton or be learned matters little to me; if we looked upon our Superiors with the eyes of faith, that is, in Jesus, we would not pay heed to so many things, and appearing before our Superiors we would imagine that we were going to Jesus, that we were hearing the commands, the reproofs from Jesus.

Tell me a little, my dear daughters: if God in person truly came down from Heaven and commanded us, with what respect, submission, humility would we stand before Him? Equally, if we had the true faith that Jesus wants from us, we ought to do likewise with our Superiors, who hold for us the place of God and through whom we have, from morning to evening, the will of God.

Let us endeavour, then, to put into practice the virtue of obedience, and next Sunday we shall explain the Chapter that follows, that is, Chapter 8.

On the mortification of Gluttony

given at Piacenza on the evening of 29 January 1871

Saint Francis de Sales, whose feast is celebrated today. It is said of him that he never grew angry except twice: once when Saint Frances de Chantal, whose direction he had, appeared before him, that Lady, with some worldly object; he then grew angry, but that Saint at once humbled herself, cast herself at his feet, stripping it off at once; and he, saint of gentleness that he was, who had brought this virtue in himself to the height of sublimity, forgave her. Another time he grew angrier still, and he carried his words by way of mortification, and strongly rebuked two Religious who, while they were in the garden, ate two fruits fallen on the ground, without permission and outside meals.

I say: if this saint, who knew perfection so well and had brought it in himself to such an heroic degree that he became a master of it, what would he have said, what would his displeasure not have been, had he seen so many times the Daughters of Saint Anne who do not know how to mortify themselves, now with the apple, now with the water that is not good, now with the coffee that is not sweet enough or is not hot enough! So too, so many times, either the soup or the main dish which by chance is sometimes not as good as they would like. I will tell you, Sisters: in what shall we be able, shall we seek to mortify ourselves, if we do not know how to do these that are so small?

All the Saints, those who before dying gave signs of an uncommon holiness, all began by mortifying themselves in gluttony. Let us take a Mariana of Jesus, who, still little and in swaddling clothes, would not take milk on Friday and on Saturday, and so many other women saints who gave signs of mortification and heroic holiness. A Saint Rose of Lima, who she too from her infancy mortified herself in all that her palate felt a desire for. There cannot be souls aspiring to perfection without their beginning to mortify themselves in this sense of taste.

I do not say that you are to imitate these extraordinary women saints, and I would not wish you to take it amiss. Yes, eat, but not to fill the sack, to satisfy your taste; rather you must put it into your head that you must eat in order to work in the House of the Lord, so as to have strength to labour for the work of God, but not for the pleasure of eating that better thing, or because it is better, to sate oneself with it, and to go so far in everything as to rid oneself of one’s own will. The community passes me a pear, an apple: be it hard, be it soft, be it unripe, be it ripe, I eat it just the same. The women saints, for fear that the sense of the flesh might rebel against the spirit and might make their flesh soft, so that it would smell of stench, never ate anything that pleased their palate, their taste, but rather went seeking those things that were most contrary, and which they went on to savour [?], and indeed sought to make them as disgusting as they could by sprinkling on them now ashes, now aloes, etc…. so that their taste would savour nothing, but only their God. But you will say to me: you speak of these things to us, who already eat so poorly? Already so badly? I will answer you that not every day, but sometimes there is that dish which most attracts the appetite; one would like to eat more of it; instead, to leave it or eat less of it: there, this is what pleases Jesus most, and what little by little leads us to perfection, and one acquires so many merits.

So too another thing: eating outside meals. I assure you these are things so contrary to a creature who wishes to tend to perfection that they make one shudder to think that a daughter makes so little account of it. Tell me, can you not keep to three meals a day? So what is done? One asks permission and, having obtained it, one eats in the pantry; one goes into the kitchen without the Superior having sent us, and there, on the pretext of tasting now one thing, now another, one eats and falls into faults against the Rule; and why does one fall? Because that enemy who is always attached to us and intent on making us fall stirs up our appetite and ends by having the victory himself. I, believe me, have been a religious for five years, by the grace of God; I go into the kitchen, into the pantry, and I can assure you, and the pantry sisters, both those who were there before and those at present, can say it, whether they have ever been able to notice that I took anything, nor did they ever see me taste the least thing outside meals; and why? Because I cannot give occasion to so many weak, less strong souls to take scandal, to form some thought, and in short be myself the cause (God deliver me from it) of their committing sin. I bring this example so that you may understand that if I encourage you and urge you to follow this so beautiful point of the Rule, it is because I know it will bring you great goods, both for the soul and for the body; for this donkey of ours too benefits greatly in its health from keeping to meals, and so you can work and labour for the glory of God.

I, you see, if I took a little thing outside meals, but without extreme need, would make a scruple of it. And why make a scruple of it? Because I know I am always in the presence of God, and I know that God sees me. On the contrary, if I took that little thing, I might give occasion to that sister to think ill, to make some judgement, I do not say through her own fault, but through that infernal enemy who leads her to it. For, you see, many years ago a person presented me with something to eat; I did not take it; but had I taken it, you see, I would have given occasion for the devil, who is so cunning, to lead her into sin; and in fact she said to me: It is true, at such a moment, at such an hour, I was thinking ill of you, if by chance you had accepted it; and she made me the most exact confession of her interior that could be made. And yet, you see, this creature loved me so much that I believe I have never had anyone who loved me as much as she did, to the point that I was afraid she idolised me, and I prayed God that I might not be the cause of taking from her the love she owed to Him; but I made sure that she loved me and saw me only in God. These are things that I must tell you for your safeguard, so that you do not let yourselves be led on by the devil. They are things that I must tell you and make known, not to all, however, but to those who are young in vocation. So too, as to what you believe, that if the Mother eats meatless food she does it for mortification: Ah! no, I can assure you; they made the experiment, but in vain, for as soon as they gave me something with meat to eat I felt like vomiting and I really did vomit; even the smell, you see, of meat has the same effect on me. It is for me indeed a greater and more painful mortification to have to eat differently from the Community, to have always to see little pots set aside for the Mother. God alone knows what pain I feel in this. This not being able to eat meat came to me from an illness.

Of another thing I must inform you, and it is that you should not be scandalised if you see me take coffee only in the morning, and in so small a dose. From girlhood I could never take breakfast as all children do, and once, when at home they forced me to take milk and coffee, they had enough of it and never spoke to me of it again, for I was taken ill at once, and having gone to church for Mass they had to take me home, where I vomited everything. When I was stronger I would remain until dinner without taking anything hot, and I did not suffer; indeed, as I have already told you, I had to do so in order to keep well. But listen: it is a year and a half that, as you see me, I am no longer good for anything, and I feel that that drop of coffee gives me a little strength, rouses my nerves and does me good. Except, however, for certain times, as for example when I was in Sampierdarena: for all that they did and begged me, both the Superior and Sr. A. Vincenza, I could not even bear the smell of coffee, and the very sight of it was repugnant to me. I was 15 and 20 years without taking coffee or breakfast, as I have already told you; I do not say that I was strong, but I did not suffer; whereas now I truly feel that it gives me a little life, that I truly need that little drop of coffee. So too with wine: I do not drink it [?], I could never take any; and when I was forced to, even at times of no small importance, if I drank it, it did not give me a stomach-ache but pain in my arms, and such pains that I could not bear them. So you see that it is not something that happens to me now that I am a Religious; indeed, I must tell you that I never ate so much as here, being obliged to; I have them all at me, and I have to eat by force many times so as not to displease them, whereas at home I did as I wished, without anyone noticing. Dear daughters, I am obliged by my Superior to tell you these things, because it is now five years that I have not spoken of them, and I must say it for the new sisters, so that, being forewarned, the devil may not tempt them to think ill and to form suspicions. But now let us return to our conference: mortify yourselves, my dear daughters, if you truly wish to become true religious. Immortification kills the creature and makes her lose all the esteem one might formerly have had; it makes her languid in all the offices of piety, of religion.

One sees this creature who prays badly, cannot stay in church, thinks of nothing else but contenting her palate, her body. When a creature is not mortified, her flesh can easily bring her to disorders, to less than chaste thoughts, even to sins. And indeed I see those who live for the Lord and those who live for the world, to content their flesh.

Enter the room of the latter, and you will begin to smell a cadaverous stench that comes out of the unclean mouth of such a one; his room smells of a thousand odours; it seems a sewer of hell, which forces you to go out. But it is not so with a bride of the Lord, who knows that every morning she is to receive Jesus into her breast. In the evening she takes care not to eat too much, so as not to have in the morning a mouth that smells of food, and so as to have her stomach clean to receive that God who is all purity, all cleanness. A Saint Philip Neri would eat nothing in the evening, so that in the morning he might have his stomach, his heart, his mouth clean to receive Jesus; and after having made his Communion he would remain until dinner time without taking food, adoring that God who was in his breast. I do not say this for you, that you should imitate it, for this was a Saint, and not all are called, as he was, to the same Holiness; but certain small mortifications, which so beautify the soul and give so much pleasure to our Jesus, and which will lead you to holiness, you can do. You will say to me: why then do not all become saints for so little? I will answer you: because not all wish to mortify themselves, because they do not mortify their little whims, their tastes, and so they will never come to mortify themselves in the big things.

I am finishing; let us endeavour to mortify ourselves, so that the spirit of immortification may not enter into us; for, you see, that person can no longer do anything good; she always thinks of tomorrow, she stays talking. Dissipated as can be, and what good can she do to her soul by doing so? All the more we, who have so dissipated a life, how shall we manage? By keeping ourselves continually in the presence of God. Tell me a little, dear daughters, how many spiritual communions do you make in a day? Today, before Communion, I had already made fifty; you too make them during the day, for these will keep you always in the presence of God, and so you will never sin.

In the particular examination at midday you can make it on the presence of God, and pray the Most High to deign to help you to acquire this beautiful gift of the presence of God.

On the importance of observing

our Holy Rules

given in Sampierdarena on the evening of 25 February 1871

It seems to me that our Holy Mother explains this point to us well enough: how important is the practice and observance of what this holy little book contains. I can assure you that it has come from no other than the hand of the Lord, and I say within myself: and can it be true that this book surpasses that of Saint Augustine and of all the other Saints who had communication with God?

And ours, which contains all exquisiteness, how shall we be able to put it into practice?

On the other hand, the thought that God has given it, that His desire, His will is that we may work at it well, study it and put it into practice, heartens and strengthens me. But you will answer me: if the prelates who have read these Holy Rules have said that it is impossible that a human person could have formed a single thought of what they contain, and that it is impossible that a human person could observe them well, how shall we be able to do it? I will answer you that what they told me did not make me fear at all, and also it never gives me any worry that you cannot put them into practice; indeed, the further you go on, the more they will become adapted to your spirit. I say within myself: is anything difficult to the Holy Spirit? Nothing. The Holy Spirit can imprint on a soul the wisdom, the spirit necessary to act well. Therefore, if to the Holy Spirit nothing is impossible, nothing difficult, it will not be that the Daughters of Saint Anne cannot put them into practice. Indeed, all the most knowledgeable persons, after having read and studied them, could find nothing in them to take away nor to add, nor any correction to make, but they say only that a creature who observes them must become a saint. It is indeed true that Saint Anne, in presenting the Holy Rules, said: none of my daughters will be lost, all will infallibly be saved, they will stay little in purgatory and will enjoy a particular glory, greater than others. Following this, I say within myself: to stay little in Purgatory they must be well adorned with virtues, since even some Saint has had to stay there some time. The Holy Spirit will give these creatures that strength, that capacity to observe them, as the persons who read these so austere Rules say. I say it is true, because all the others, those of a Saint Clare, of the Chantal, none bring one to that high sublimity of perfection, of humility, as these do. Let us take Poverty and see to what sublimity it is brought: we have nothing, everything can be taken from us, and blessed will be that Daughter of Saint Anne who is able to put it into practice. You will tell me that those Sisters who died and are already in Paradise, of whom we already have four, did not do great things. I will answer you that a single hour, a single day of observing them all is enough to save us. As you see, we live on providence, but so great is the confidence I have in God that I have never prayed for it; in the end they made me observe that I ought to ask God for it, and then I began to pray, I do not say much, but I pray and recommend myself to the prayers of good souls; I have also had prayers said in our Houses, but listen, we are always the same; perhaps it will be my sins, perhaps, because we have never imbibed this Vow of Poverty, God makes us put it into practice by force. Of all the sisters we have in Paradise, among the sins they had to expiate the first was Poverty; nothing was able to free her [?]. She had to expiate them by herself. And this was told me by a good soul: that these sisters of ours could not do otherwise than expiate them by themselves. Hearing this, I understand that if God gave us more, we would make ourselves showy rooms, and who knows what we would do; I first of all would go into the first Class [?], if God did not keep His Most Holy Hand upon my head. I feel sorrow over it and I say to the Lord: send us a little providence, not so that we may not have to work, but so that we may eat reasonably. I always think: why must those Houses that are going to be founded eat a crust of bread and the others more? Oh, no, they must all be equal. You see, we are already more than a hundred persons and we have always gone forward with providence.

We have found ourselves, it is true, with nothing, but at the moment of paying the bills the money comes to us. And is this not all the providence of the Lord? The Lord wishes us to observe poverty in want [?], so that afterwards in greatness we may know how to put it into practice. The person who knows how to put it into practice in narrowness of means will find it the same to practise it in prosperity; whereas those who in narrowness let everything go to waste and make no account of anything, partly through diabolical suggestions, partly through their bad habits, how much will they waste in abundance? But this is not enough: we are obliged to put this Vow into practice scrupulously in order to acquire its virtue; and Jesus Himself, although born in Nazareth in a stable, in the utmost poverty, willed to observe this virtue all the more, going afterwards in search of a crust of bread. But where am I carrying myself? We wanted to consider the observance of the Holy Rules and the Fruit we shall draw from them. The fruit will be the eternal crown: whoever has put them into practice more will have more glory, whoever less, less glory. You will say to me: but they are so subtle that it is a real martyrdom. I will answer you: what did the martyrs do to acquire that crown, that glory which they now enjoy? Let us then endeavour to study them well, not only to keep them in our pocket, as we do. Apropos of this, listen: there are no Religious Orders in which each Religious may keep their Rules; there is no Community. With the Sisters of Charity, the Superior keeps one copy; in the other Religious Orders, from time to time the Superior reads them aloud and nothing more; but none may keep them in her pocket. So fine is the holiness that the Holy Mother wishes to instil in us that we have all the more need to look at them often.

The Vow of obedience is brought to the summit of perfection, for it comprises not only obedience in itself, but also the total death of ourselves.

The nurse must obey when she is sent to the sick person; tomorrow the superior takes her away and she must no longer go there; she is placed in another office and she must obey.

She is sent again to the sick person and she goes. The Rules of the Nurses are now being printed; they are so beautiful that one cannot imagine it. So you see, all this is new and has nothing to do with the other Religious Orders, and it is so sublime that it makes such an impression on a person living in the World that it seems to her that whoever puts them into practice must be a Seraph. But we must not be discouraged by this; we must hold firm in ourselves that faith, that with the help of God nothing is ever difficult, but everything with His grace becomes easy. We must hold firm in this faith: that if God has placed me here, if He has given me this holy little book, I must be certain that He will give me the strength to observe what it contains and to become a saint. And who is greater than this Order, which is under the power of a mighty God whom nothing equals, and we are His daughters?

And if Saint Anne is so dear to God, so near to Him, for having given the human race the divine Redeemer; and if Saint Anne was looked upon by the Eternal Father with such delight, we who are her daughters, what will be the love she will bear us? How dear shall we be to her heart? No Institute makes the month of the Eternal Father, and we do it. So, courage! The Holy Pope Pius IX told me: we shall be like so many apostles, our Institute will spread to all parts of the world; so how can I have a speck of mistrust? How can I fear, having this before my eyes? I pray that God may send us a little providence, but not for anything else. At Piacenza we go to the assistance of the sick with the applause of all; the Bishop blessed us, and even the worst listen to us, and this by the mercy of God. One sees that the Holy Mother has stripped us of truly everything; we know nothing of worldly intrigues. The nurses go with assurance into the houses and are seen by all without fear. You see, I alone know what scrutiny we had at the beginning. Certain people sifted us, so to speak; they knew better than I myself what went on in the House; but now all that is over, and not only do they leave us in peace, but they carry us, so to speak, in the palm of their hand.

So must not all this be for us a proof that everything is the work of God, so that we may observe them well? And with what (earnestness) must we put them into practice! You will tell me that we go slowly; you are right; but do you know how long a Saint Vincent de Paul waited after having founded the first House? And to have the approval, do you know how long he waited? He already had 200 houses and his rule was not yet approved; and we instead run under full sail without my doing anything.

Yes, I shall always say it, and I can confirm it, that I have done nothing for this Work. The Lord has done everything; I am nothing but a poor donkey, good for nothing, so that when I think of it I shudder; and when some person recommends himself to my prayers, they make me tremble, knowing that I am the most wicked of all. But the thought that my prayers are united to yours gives me courage; and even if I were a double Magdalene, I ought to be certain of pardon; and I would have to be wicked indeed if I were not sure of Paradise, because if my sins deserve hell, the mercy of God covers and defends all.

On the evening of 12 March 1871

on Poverty

What more beautiful grace have we than to be able to put into practice the Vow of Poverty! All the Daughters of Saint Anne have scope [?] to put it into practice; but how they observe it, my God! I see and understand well that if God keeps us so very low, He does it because who knows, if we were richer, how we would put into practice this Vow which God loves so much? And indeed, did not God Himself practise it? He, Master of Heaven and earth, did He not will to be born poor of a poor virgin, not having even wherewith to cover Himself? And if the Son of God practised it in coming upon this earth, can we not say that this Vow is pleasing to the Eternal Father?

And if the Son, who possessed everything, left everything: born of Royal Lineage, of a virgin herself also of royal lineage, He willed to be born at a moment in which she was deprived of everything. Tell me, if I love a person, shall I not do everything to content that person? And if it is true that we love God, how must we not put into practice this Vow which God loves so much, and the observance of which He so longs for from us? What happiness we would feel in saying: I have succeeded in giving pleasure to my God! We see the Saints, who were all eyes, all ears, so that the goods of God might not be lost. For example, the wardrobe sister, the pantry sister, takes care that this stuff, this thing, that other, is not lost. Let us go into the Workroom: I see this needleful of thread being lost. This pin (on) the ground: even if it is not my obligation, even if I am not the wardrobe sister, still I must look to it and put it away, so that it is not lost. I see this stuff being lost, being spoilt: I must pick it up, put it in order; thus I shall do two offices, my own, and I shall preserve the goods of the Lord.

The Lord teaches it to me, the Vow of Poverty. The pot that is boiling needs less wood: I take care at once to remove a piece or two, and so it will serve me to make another boil. Oh! Yes, we shall see at the Tribunal of God, when He asks us to account for what we have wasted, for the little attention we have paid to observing this Vow of Holy Poverty.

So, for example: I have an old dress; must I perhaps not patch it any more? Yes, and how! I must ask the Superior for a piece of cloth and sew it, patch it to the very last. See how many times the Lord permits it, causing the Superiors not to notice that that sister has an old dress, so that she may put this Vow more into practice by patching it, sewing it, and not wait to come into Church losing a rag on one side, a ribbon on the other, and needing the Superior to come and tell her to sew her dress. See what came into my mind; listen: coming down here, I saw that the Superior put a new dress into the trunk, and in the night I was thinking: I shall give this dress away and take her old one, and by dint of patches I shall sew it, put it on and go out with that sister who seems to suffer at going out, and go to Genova with that sister who is poorly dressed, or who is united [?]; but what would you? Because of a circumstance I had suddenly to go out; otherwise I would truly have done it; this was really the true way of putting into practice the Vow of Poverty. Once, listen, there was a person who was kept so strictly that if she wanted something she had to go and ask for it: it happened that her shoes tore, and she sewed them herself so as not to be always asking, and she was so content to wear those shoes that she would no longer wear any others, new ones. Another time this same person ran short of skirts and was without them; why? Because, while she was sewing them for herself and had no others, a poor woman knocked at the door who was without a shift; she at once left off sewing them and gave them to her. How many of these souls there are in the World who, without making the Vow of poverty, put this virtue into practice and are the support of their homes; they are truly a consolation.

There was a person who every morning ate a crust of bread, and she had asked her family’s permission that every time they rang at the door they should let her go and open it; and it seemed that the Lord did it on purpose: just as she was about to eat that crust of bread, there was a knock, and it was a poor man; she gave him her bread, remaining fasting the whole day; she always did it, of course with the permission of her Director. And shall we not be able to make some privation for our little girls? For example: today at table the fruit was not passed round, so as to give it to the girls. Everything, my dear daughters, can be done; the rest is idle talk; and even if I saw one going into ecstasy who did not have charity, I would say she is a Cepinetto [?], because she is not then able to make a mortification. A religious, by observing her Rules, can become a saint, for she is in continual mortification. Today I go to table: whether there be salad, fruit, bread, I eat all the same. What is done for appearance is never holiness, and those mortifications which she seeks to make seen are worth nothing to her. I always say to the Lord: yes, if I were in a position to have a little sweet and the sisters could notice it, I would say to the Lord: for charity’s sake, take it from me at once, because I know that I am so frail, I am filth, I have never measured myself with anyone, I could fall into pride, believe myself thereby more than I am, and lose every good I might have. We know it: we are all children of Adam. So everything that is of appearance, of exteriority, take it from me, my God, for all is pride, self-love. Lucifer too was an angel, and through pride he fell and became the worst of all the devils. I have heard so many of them say: the Lord speaks to me, tells me, shows me… and then touch their skirt and you will hear. One of these said to me one day: and do you not believe in these things? How many of them I have seen, and I know that as long as they are given good things they are all sweetness; but I say: there you have balloons of hell; cross them a little, try telling them something, and either they no longer look at you, or you are done with them for good.

Given at Sampierdarena

on the evening of 14 March 1872

on the love of God

Human tongue is not able to explain what the love of God is; let us begin by searching in the books that speak of this love, or else let us ask the Philosophers, the moralists and the ascetical writers who unravel so well the mysteries and Sacred Scripture, yet they will be able to define nothing for us on this. And yet they studied Moses in the burning bush, while in that bush so many wonders were wrought. I am not capable of speaking to you of this from Sacred Scripture. It is called a bush, this you know; so too of David everything is explained to us very well, but this matter is too hidden. We have, moreover, a great many Masters of the spirit who set themselves to unravel, to reason subtly about what the love of God is; never have they been able to succeed in explaining it, nor the sweetness of this love; they wished to liken it to a zephyr which, as it draws near us, makes us burn; they wished to liken it to a burning fire… in part they took it from the Seraphim, but we do not find it described in books as those blessed and fortunate souls who possess it, who live immersed in it and enjoy an anticipated paradise, feel it and know how to express it. One who wrote well of this was a St. Catherine of Genoa; she expresses the love of God with vividness; we see a St. Catherine unlettered, yet divine knowledge made her describe it very well; we see a St. Teresa, that Seraph of love, whose sayings and writings could only have come from heavenly dictation; she explains it clearly, she details its particular features very well. St. Catherine of Genoa, little instructed as she was, also expresses it with the most vivid signs, with words whose every stroke expresses the love she felt. It means, then, that neither learning nor the mind of man is needed to understand what this love is, which can be had from God alone, and that one is not able to describe it unless one has tasted it. But you will say to me: then if we do not experience this love we shall never be able to say what it is? It is true, dear daughters. St. Francis, a common man and of little capacity: his little songs were all declarations of love of what he felt. St. Philip Neri, so great was the vividness, the fire of the love of God that he nourished in his breast, was many times obliged to cry out. Stop, my God, stop, he would cry, for I am dying; and like one mad, in the streets and in his room, he would say: My God, go away from me, for You are making me die.

But that is not enough, you will tell me: if it is a thing that the learned and the philosophers cannot describe, but only the Seraphim, the Saints, and not all the Saints, shall we never be able to understand it, never taste it? Yes: God says to the creature: strip yourself of yourself, give your will into the hands of your Superiors. It is your will that forms a wall against the love of God. You will say to me: these are free gifts that God gives to whomever He pleases. I will answer you: and could it not be that He would give these graces to us too?

But to obtain it three things are needed, three points to observe: the first is prayer; the second, the stripping of one’s own will, telling God to set His heel upon it, so that we no longer live by ourselves but by the will of God, which is that of our Superiors, whereby we are as dead to ourselves; and then, when we have reached this stripping, this death, God will make Himself felt by us and we shall taste a little of His love. Then sometimes it happens that with some creature God is pleased to play, after having ensnared her with His love. All of a sudden He withdraws. Alas! This soul passes into a painful state; she no longer feels anything; distracted, dry at Communion, a thousand thoughts torment her. She will say, then, with sorrow: so I no longer belong to God; I must have given Him occasion to withdraw from me. When we have examined our actions and found nothing grave, then let her believe that God is playing with her. St. Teresa used to say that she was very glad in dryness, because that time was a preparation for some consolation and sweetness; but after these sweetnesses God would again leave her dry and suffering anew. This is the purging of the soul.

The bride of the Canticle, who was all inebriated with the love of God, lamented because Jesus had abandoned her. My Beloved, she exclaimed, why have You left me so alone? Jesus answered her: I was always near you, I heard your laments, I saw your suffering, I heard your laments, I saw your suffering, and with My support you were able to bear everything; and she walked swiftly in the way of the Lord.

So you see, it is in dryness that great strides are made in the way of God. But you will say to me: we want to feel, to taste something of the love of God. You are right; but you know that a soul that wants to sanctify herself does not ask God for sweetness, but for suffering. As for me, I am not yet good at suffering.

The love of God is so strong that the soul would burn up if God with His omnipotence did not sustain her, and indeed it is a fire that consumes, that reduces to ashes; and St. Philip Neri, who possessed it so much, used to say: quick, give me water, for I am burning; and he went about the house like a madman, and had he let himself go where his mind wished, he would have died burnt, so great was the fire that consumed him. He had to distract himself, to sing, to do foolish things so as not to feel, to quench the living flame of the love of God that he had in his breast and that burned him. These things I know from having read them in books and not by any other way. Now I will tell you how this fire enters the soul of the creature. Sometimes a creature goes to Communion dry, without sensible fervour; she goes out of obedience; and yet, to give her proof of how dear obedience is to Him, the Lord lets her taste a little of His caresses; well, many times in this Communion the Lord gives His love. Once the Lord had done a great many graces to a soul, but He had not yet given her His love; going to Communion she was thinking of her faults, annihilated; she was asking the Lord for pity and mercy, and so the poor thing remained.

All of a sudden an arrow strikes her in the heart; her left arm burns. She does not know what to do in such a state; she cannot go out.

All of a sudden she falls asleep, she rejoices, she exults, she feels her God within herself, she sees His heart, she feels, she feels the flames of the fire of her God burning her.

In such a state she no longer feels anything human; they prick her, they shake her; she is motionless, she is insensible, and in such a way that if God did not withdraw little by little she would die. Finally she sees the arms of her God stripped of flesh, she sees the hole, the blood from the hands,

those piercings of the wounds; she sees her God, she feels Him, she tastes Him, and in that moment her body is dead to the earth. You will say to me: why, if she was asleep, did she not wake while they were shaking her? No, because all her senses were with her God; she was enjoying her Beloved and no longer lived to the earth. Oh, blessed one! She no longer knew anything of earth or of what is human, but feels herself ever immersed in God. Little by little she comes back, and the time that passed while she was in that state always seems to her less than a second. If she is asked whether she is suffering, she does not know what to answer, because she knows nothing any more, and it seems to her but a second since she received her God.

When He has withdrawn from this soul, there remains to her nothing but a strength that would defy the whole world. And you will say to me: had she not experienced dryness? I will answer you: we do not know; what is certain is that God always tests first with dryness, with temptations; it is rare that God leads a soul into such states without first having tested her. You will say to me: if we had experienced this love, we too would be afraid of nothing, we would defy the whole world. Ah! No, poor thing, this strength does not always last for her, no; because, having tasted this love, when she comes into dryness she suffers more than before, when she had not yet experienced this love; she writhes, she dies of sorrow. We see a St. Mary Magdalene de’ Pazzi who, after having enjoyed God, and therefore knowing Him ever more, felt the pain ever more strongly when He left her dry. The most obscene things, indecent thoughts came to torment her, while we know that she was innocent and knew nothing of the world, and God wished to test her in order to lead her higher still than before. Nothing but obedience could make her go to Communion. My God, she would say, how can I go to Communion with such obscene things before my eyes? Obedience, obedience! Ah! Sisters, put these things out of your minds, saying: if I had experienced this love of God I would be ready for anything. We say this in church in the fervour of a little devotion; but then, when that moment has passed, are we capable of bearing the rudeness of that sister, that reproof given with too much heat? I shall be at the bedside of a sick person to serve him; shall I feel ready, shall I be capable of receiving from him blows and ill-treatment, and of treating him with charity, serving him with more love, with more assiduity? Shall I be a St. Catherine of Siena, who, while she was serving a sick woman, was insulted by her, and the woman ended by saying of her the most obscene things that could be imagined? What did Catherine do? She went on tending her with love, with more zeal than before, so that that woman, overcome by such virtue, humbled herself before Catherine, saying to her: O God, what have I done to you! Is this how I repay you for the good you do me? And she always loved her, esteemed her and is her friend. To speak of this love, of the exquisiteness of this love, a whole lifetime would not suffice.

Well then, she who does not feel the love of God cannot meditate, cannot taste; but you see, for a Religious it is easier for Jesus to give her a taste of His divine love than for a person in the world, because God, you see, gives Himself wholly to a religious; He loves her, He caresses her, He lets her taste Himself; indeed we see in the lives of the Saints that many are Religious and few married. God, God has always shown us that if He wanted some person to be a saint for the Altars, if they were married they were left widowed, or else for the most part they were religious, because the Church puts fewer obstacles, because she knows that God has a special predilection for Religious. Take courage, then, be spurred on in the way of perfection and acquire what I tell you; but I recommend humility to you. I have observed many times that those religious, you see, full of self-love and of wanting to appear more than they are, God humbles them by making them appear more than they are, God humbles them by making everything they do turn out badly. You see, I have had dealings with Religious, those full of self-love, of the esteem of others: in all the embroideries, the works that they believed to be well done and for which they expected to receive praise, on presenting them, the Lord, to humble them, made them appear full of mistakes and badly executed.

On the contrary, you see, that humble person God seeks to exalt. I will tell you of a fact. A person in Genoa, humble as could be, was ordered to do a piece of work in gold [?] which she had never done; she did it, she carried it out, and when it was presented it was seen by Priests, by persons of talent, and was found most beautiful. God did this to test her humility, and so He will do with us. I would have so many facts to tell you that I would never finish, but I only tell you that it is the truth of the Gospel that whoever humbles himself shall be exalted and whoever exalts himself shall be humbled.

given at Ferrara on the evening of 16 March 1872

On various points of the Rule

Since you desire it, I will tell you something, not to scold you but so that you may know how to conduct yourselves; first, on that point of being able to write to the Mother. You already know how one must write, both of temporal and of spiritual things. I am leaving one sister charged with collecting the letters. You will say to this sister: I wish to write to the Mother; and she will give you the paper; when you have written it you will present it to her, and she will seal it in your presence and will be obliged to put it in the post. If she should be ill, you infirmarians drop it in the post yourselves, but first you show it to the Superior: this is so in all the houses; because, let us suppose, for example, that a sister has had some greater compunction at Communion and wrote of it to the Mother; the Superior, reading the letter, might say: oh! she is writing about her ecstasies; so, to remove every suspicion, they will give it to the sister as I told you above. Suppose you are angry: do not write at once, wait until you are quite calm; for example, something happens to you: I will write about it, one says in one’s heart, and one waits two or three days and then writes and gives it to the sister to post; and be sure, believe me, that no one reads your letters, for when there is something of the spirit in them or of your troubles, I burn them, I give them to the flames, because of this, believe me, I have always made a great scruple. You may also drop it in the post without a stamp, without showing it to anyone.

As for silence, I observed that it is not kept; the strict silence after ten o’clock is kept fairly well, but that of the morning not at all, because it is known that the Mother is in her room and does not hear. And it is not known that the Mother is watching from one hole and another to make quite sure of it. So I asked whether the bell is rung for rising, for the morning silence, at half past seven, and I was told no! So too I observed that silence is broken in the recreation room; and I was told that you go to recreation in the building works, on the scaffolding, at the windows: things that have torn my heart.

Sisters, you are the seeds of our Institute; on you, on the first ones, depends the whole good success of the others. This confirms for me the suspicions that arose in me in Rome, and you know, I have wept more than once, not with my eyes but with my heart. In the Recreation room you may laugh, but not in the building works where everyone hears you. Dear daughters, let us observe modesty; this Chapter of our Holy Rules, which explains it so well, why have you not studied it, when you had them in your pocket? From this I gather that there will not have been even the mitigated silence, and I was astonished that yesterday, as I passed among you all, you told me nothing; not one of you spoke to me of it. So you will have let something be overheard, because people outside told me things that are our internal affairs.

For charity’s sake I recommend silence to you; be patient, we are surrounded by a hundred eyes. Do you want to laugh? Find yourselves a place where no one can see you, and there laugh, talk. You will say to me: where are we to go? You may first go into the building works, as I used to take you, to take a turn, and then come back into this room, shut yourselves in, and there laugh, talk. Then tell me a little: have you done here as is done in Piacenza for the change of linen?

In winter the chemises once a week, and twice in summer? Likewise two collars. I hope you have all understood how you must conduct yourselves, and still more, because, you see, everyone now has their eyes on you, and it is from you that I may have joys or great sorrows, because now they are about to approve our Institute, and here in Ferrara especially they are watching all your steps, your ways. So in the street, at the homes of the sick, you must observe your Rules as if you had them in your pocket, for everyone looks at you, observes you; and if you do as I tell you, you will be that seed which will sprout in this house, which in the course of time will become a great foundation, and God will bless your labours; you will find yourselves crowned with a crown far more resplendent than the others. I hope that you will obey me, and that I shall have nothing to do another time but congratulate you, blessing the Lord in all His designs.

given at Ferrara on her return from Rome

The Superior has the rules; you must take care to study them and still more to observe them and put them into practice, for now that you have them anew you have bound yourselves.

I recommend to you the works of piety; do them with fervour, for without prayer there can be nothing good; likewise at Meditation, all be ready, and indeed take care to be in church before the bell, so as to have time to say some prayer. Be ready at the first stroke of the bell, leave everything and run where obedience calls her.

Believe that a Religious who is ready for her office, ready for the obedience of the Superior, is sure of paradise, for all the other virtues come after. Observe that on the day when we are not ready for meditation at the sound of the bell, nothing will go well during the day.
