In the acts of community we have our sanctification; we have a blessed Berchmans who sanctified himself by obedience, by the observance of his Rules and of the timetable. I hear the bell and it calls me to prayer; I must leave everything and go there at once: that religious who in the morning rises promptly at the first stroke and goes to Church, and there pours out her heart to her God in loving thanksgiving.

The second point is to go composed in the streets, not to talk; I have told you so many times that a daughter of Saint Anne must be, by her modesty, the edification of people.

I recommend to you also the care of the sick: go to them with love, with reverence, as if going to Jesus; if sleep comes upon me, I will take care to get up and do everything possible to wake myself; I must imagine myself to be before Jesus, who counts everything I do for this sick person. You see, I went for 25 years and it seemed to me that I was going to paradise; you see, there is no consolation on earth like this; I have not experienced any more since I no longer go. Yes, do everything with spirit. I am in this Hospital; this woman full of vermin, I dress her wounds, I relieve her: ah! What delight to think of relieving a creature of Jesus! Yes, there is no office that brings so much consolation as this: to come back home in the morning and say, I have dressed the wound of my Jesus! You will say to me: but I have not experienced these delights. Ah! Because it means that you have never done it with spirit; why do we let so many labours go to waste, why do we act as if we were so many servants?

Ah! Yes, the Lord has always looked upon the infirmarians with an eye of predilection. Likewise the teachers: take care that the girls learn their catechism well. The Lord has given me 20, 30 girls to look after; well, I want them to become good and dear to God; it may be that one day they will be Religious.

Ah! [?] these little girls, how rough and naughty they are! Ah! We cannot say so, for whoever loves God must seek that all these hearts love God; if these hearts have grown up without knowing God, in the mire of the earth, well then, let us overturn these hearts, winning them for God; let us cleanse them with our care, so that the creature will love her God, will come out of her lethargy and will begin to live in God. Yes, because whoever has understanding loves God. Yes, the teacher must draw the heart of all creatures; yes, I will absorb the hearts of all the little girls, so that when they leave school they will say: ah! Come to my school; there God is known, there one enjoys a peace never enjoyed before; there is a teacher there who draws all hearts.

You see, I tell you these things because I have experienced them; I had a Parish under me and they all loved me. You will say to me: but in Ferrara they are naughty, they have never had a father, a mother. Enough: she has a heart; steal it from her and you will do with her whatever you wish; do not do this so that these little girls love me, no; for God, your Jesus, say to Him: I give You this heart which I have stolen for You, which loves You, knows You. Yes, steal her heart and you will do with her as much as you wish. Yes, seek to steal her heart for God.

What pain at the last judgement to think: how many hearts I could have given to Jesus, and instead how many have been lost through my fault. You must draw them with gentleness, because bees are caught with honey. What sorrow I felt in these days in thinking that before there were 200 girls and now there are fewer than a hundred. God will have accepted my suffering in these days, I hope. Enough: renew your resolutions and take care to act in such a way that the little girls come back again to our schools; I hope so.

given at Ferrara on the evening of 2 March 1872

on the mutual love that the Daughters of Saint Anne

must have among themselves

Mutual love among the daughters of Saint Anne ought to be so lively that it should never need to be urged; their very being ought to be full of mutual love, one for the other. But instead I say with sorrow: My God, why in this Your House, where it ought to be rooted with roots so firm as never to be torn up, yet alas I must say to God that this Charity seems altogether dead among you. Charity is the noblest virtue, because whoever possesses it has a noble and sensitive heart.

But why then, I always say to my God, such dryness, that your heart has a band of sourness? Why does it not have that band of love, not carnal, but full of Charity? If you were to say, when speaking with one another: my God, this one with whom I am speaking is not a creature like the others, but You have given her to me so that she may be my spiritual companion, and in You I must always see and love her.

Instead we let that carnal and sensual band take root. O wretched ones! And why, my God, do You not give these hearts a drop of this virtue which You love so much, and without which one cannot enter Paradise? I reasoned it out and said: because we are deaf to His voice; we hear that inspiration which says to us: go, serve her, she is your sister; yes, she is your sister in Jesus Christ; love her with a love wholly divine, pure, spiritual, so that you may both then enjoy the same glory in Paradise. Ah! Sisters, if there were this love, there would not be those partialities, those envies; seeing that sister who is beginning to practise virtue, that suspicion would not arise in us: she is a pretender; or seeing the Superior do something more for a sister, show her some consideration, to say: this one is the Superior’s pet. Is a sister ill? There would arise in us the desire to help her, to relieve her. Would the thought come to us of calling a Sister “Sister So-and-so”, changing her name as a joke and a jest, or of making our recreation at the expense of one Sister or another? Our recreation, as our Holy Rules say, must be cheerful, but without going on to tax one Sister and another with certain points. Enough: let us leave the past and come to the present, seeing whether this fault is there, and let us seek to remove it; let us pray God to fill us with charity; let us love our sisters, lavishing on them with love what they need, helping them, comforting them in the sorrows they may have. See that your heart is all eagerness for the Sisters. Ah! Yes, then. You will be so full of love that you will no longer see any defect in your sisters. You must spur one another on in observance, and act so that that sister who is not very observant may, by your example, become observant. You see a sister who has a defect: at once turn your gaze upon yourselves, saying: oh, how many more I have than she! For example, another will come who goes to the door, and one sees that she stops to chatter. What does one do? At once one corrects her with love, saying to her: Sister, it seems to me you are not doing well, you are failing against the Rule. Then what does this Sister do? She answers: you are right. Ah! If you do so, what a Community of Angels this would be, which would no longer tear the heart of your Superiors. If you knew how much sorrow your Holy Mother Saint Anne feels, who would wish you all one heart, all one single will. Dear daughters, for charity’s sake, be all in agreement; ask Saint Joseph in this month to give you that affection, that lovingness which you knew so well how to enjoy in your family, which you drew so well from Jesus and from Mary. Yes, we derive from your family, we belong to Jesus, we are His Brides; and who are nearer to Jesus than His Brides? Ah! Yes, Jesus, grant us this grace. Our dear Saint Joseph, obtain it for us by your intercession. Let us put this into practice.

Given in the house of Genoa

On humility and charity

Humility and charity are most principal points of our life of perfection; certainly charity cannot go separated from humility. That religious whose heart blazes with charity is that religious who in everything finds a way to humble herself and seeks to be humbled. She sees a religious who has the most humiliating office of the House: what does this religious do? She helps her for a quarter of an hour, knowing that her Rules permit her to help her without permission. She asks obedience to go to a Sister who is ill, and sees, for example, that the infirmarian cannot arrange her bed well; she does it for her with all affection, with a heart throbbing with love, with a word of resignation to relieve her of her pain, and she is far from letting it be noticed that perhaps her flesh smells of some stench, and from saying: my God, what a smell, one cannot stay in this room, my God, how disgusting. No, I cannot believe that this reigns among you, because then I could say with sorrow: my God, with what charity you go to the sick! My God, it would no longer be the spirit of God that leads you there, but other spirits. That of vainglory: our heart is full of passions, it cannot live without loving. But the Religious has dispossessed it of all this love of vainglory, of the world; she has filled it with charity, which makes her live wholly for others, to relieve the miseries of her neighbours. We see that Gentleman whose heart is filled with charity: he goes to the hospital, washes the feet of the poor sick, has words of comfort for all; he goes into the poor houses, lowers himself into that filth, into that poverty; the spirit of charity and of humility leads him to succour those poor ones. Behold these two sisters, who like twins of one blood cannot live one without the other; instead we see the proud man who cannot bear such things and says: what, I have to go to such people? Oh! I will send someone else; as we see in our times that whoever does a little charity is held up to ridicule, and nothing reigns in the world but pride and vainglory! But in the daughters of Saint Anne these virtues must make themselves felt so vividly that one cannot live without the other. Charity–humility.

But how can it be that a daughter of Saint Anne is without charity? I cannot believe that the superior has to make such reproofs, but rather that she has to put a bridle on to restrain this love. So how can I succeed in explaining this virtue, which will shed consolation over your last moments; and God, seeing you adorned with it, cannot but receive you into His Bosom and give you a fine place in Paradise; the Church tells us so. So you see how many beautiful things this beautiful virtue brings: she who has possessed more charity will have a more beautiful place in Paradise. St. Aloysius, when he cared for the sick, always sought for himself the most loathsome, those who most filled him with revulsion, and went sucking their wounds. This is a precious gift that we must ask of God with all our strength and with our whole selves, that God may grant it to you all, as I desire with all my heart.

given at Genoa

on 31 March 1872

If poverty was embraced by Our Lord J. C. as the greatest treasure, which He loved so much, how much must we seek to practise it! The master of heaven and earth, lowered, humbled: His poverty was such that we see Him, when He was on this earth, going begging from door to door, asking for a piece of bread. Going to Calvary we see Him thirsty, deprived even of a drop of water; on the cross He had no one to support His Head crowned with thorns. Oh! poverty, if a God who could have all kingdoms sought you, then in you there is something delightful that no one knows.

My God, King of Heaven and earth, all kingdoms, all royal mantles rich with gold are Yours, and yet I see You without a tunic with which to cover Yourself. So I will always repeat: poverty, how great you are.

You will say to me: a thing that is nothing, you call great! Yes, if a God chose it, how much must a Religious love it, whom God has placed to practise it in His House. She who lives in the dwelling of the Lord.

How fortunate we shall be if we take care to put it into practice, to love it, to drink it in, in the dwelling of the Lord. He has placed poverty in His house as Queen, establishing the vow of it. The founders set it as the base of their foundations.

And what does vow mean? It is to attach oneself, to bind oneself fast to a thing; the vow says to you: I tie you to this, and while you are patched, those patches will be so many stars that will shine in Heaven.

See, I, poor in a Sepulchre, wrapped in a shroud; but then you see Me in heaven glorious and triumphant, all Paradise humbling itself before Me, all the blessed hosts; all around Him enjoy His beatitude. And what does He do? He inebriates, He imparadises all with His presence, with His love.

Today all say: our God is risen, singing hymns of glory. Yes, let us call poverty Queen, because whoever has the good fortune to embrace it here on earth, it will be she who will set the crown of glory on her head in Paradise. Those who have embraced it closely will draw nearer to our Lord J. C. Yes, O Lord, if that Religious does not take the trouble to patch it, to clean it, saying: so it changes colour and the superior is obliged to make me a new one; thus, O God, how much this Religious fails against poverty, and so one sees that great body of hers dressed in new clothes. 1st, we must take care to use every diligence that our habit may last us. 2nd, we must take care to see that nothing is spoiled; for example, if the wardrobe-keeper is out, is not at home, I see thread on the floor, things that are not in their place and that may be spoiled: I must pick them up, put them in their place; I know that my Rules permit me this for a quarter of an hour; likewise, I see a bed that is breaking: shall I let it break altogether? I must mend it, and not say: it is not my business, it is not my office. Oh! what pain it is to hear this. But I do not yet have the vow. And are you not in the House of Saint Anne, and what did you come to do in religion if not to enjoy its delights? So let us profit by this beautiful treasure, so holy that no words are to be found to express

How great this treasure is. The Church teaches it to me, and J. C. Himself, with His own person, willed to teach us not by word but by His very example, so that we too may set our feet where He set His. Truly there is poverty in our Houses, but you know why we do not yet know how to love this virtue and practise it: if we go, for example, to a rich monastery, you will see how quickly one adapts oneself well; but on the contrary, where there is Poverty, you will be able to tell me how much one suffers in having to adapt oneself; oh! where there is Poverty, you will be able to tell me how much one suffers in having to adapt oneself; oh! how much this body, which desires softness, has to suffer. Some will believe they have attained it because perhaps they have a hard straw mattress, or an old mattress, or such things. No, do not believe it, because the Saints themselves had to suffer from it. There was, you see, a person who, in short, led a holy life and for many years had accustomed her palate to eating filthy things, in short to everything, and had no longer tasted things that could bring pleasure to her palate. She goes to a place, she sees a loathsome thing; it comes into her mind that it has been put there for her, and at once she thinks of not eating it. What happened? A voice of the Lord says to her: what are you doing? What do you expect? This was enough for her for her whole life. Another person, who had taken as companion St. Francis of Assisi, who was the greatest imitator of the poverty of Jesus Christ, used to say: you who went in search of dirty, nauseating things to eat them and mortify your palate, and shall I not seek to imitate you and mortify this ugly sense of the palate? And this was enough for her to flee every delicacy. Let us too say to our St. Francis: O dear Saint, you in Paradise have the place nearest to our Lord, and why? Because you were the greatest imitator of Our Lord, you who went from door to door asking for a piece of bread and a little oil for our Lord, crying out: My Lord has no oil. Let us seek, then, to imitate the Saints in poverty, humility and Chastity and obedience, who obeyed the lowest of this earth; let us not think we are something, but rather the last of all.

On 7 April 1872

First the Mother began by saying: I must say something that I observed, namely, not to keep any things under the bed and not to change without permission; so if one had to change one’s stockings or something, ask permission of the Superior. I must recommend cleanliness. A religious must keep herself clean. The Lord is pleased that His brides be clean, but not smartly dressed, nor that they have new habits and new veils, but that they be clean, without stains, since to wash one needs soap, and one fails against poverty by consuming it; and likewise keep nothing in the room. You see, I have scruples about keeping even the towel; if I have put the numbers on the linen, it is for the sake of order, but not for any other reason; we have nothing. Before changing, for example, were it a pair of stockings, we must not go to the wardrobe-keeper, because she is not mistress to give anything; she only has the things in her keeping; but one must go to the Superior. I will give the case: I have a pair of wet stockings; I go to the Superior, I ask her for a clean pair; she tells the wardrobe-keeper; the wardrobe-keeper forgets to give them to us: must I take them myself? No, you will tell me, but I am keeping them wet, I shall catch an illness keeping them on. Enough: if you have caught it through obedience, you will have the merit of this submission in Paradise. Likewise the dispenser must not give anything without the permission of the Superior, not even a crust of bread.

You will say to me: but if she is a Superior of iron? — which, thanks be to God, has never happened among us — but let us suppose the case, you will say to me: so must we let a sister die so as not to give her a glass of wine? No, give her the glass of wine by all means; charity saves you; there remains to you, however, only the duty of making it known to the major Superiors. Then I recommend cleanliness in particular. See, O Sisters, we are poor by the grace of God, but not for all that must we go about dirty; God is pleased with cleanliness. For example, I find dirt in the House: must I go to the Superior? No; all the sisters have their offices; I must go to them. The wardrobe-keeper has in her keeping the linen and the workroom; I find the linen spoiled and dirty on the floor: to whom shall I go? To the wardrobe-keeper, and to her I will make the due reproofs. She will answer me: I have no time. Well then, I will give you help, but she will have to do the penance. Likewise I find a dirty room: I will think of the one who has it in her keeping, because she also failed against dear poverty: you have spoiled even the floor, which belongs to God. The Superior must watch over and not do, but rather punish if she does not find things well. So too the dispenser, the Sacristan, the Mistress of the girls whom we have in our care: how we must watch over the things of these little angels whom God has entrusted to us. So you must be careful to do your office well, wherever you are placed, because everything is given you by God, and from the moment obedience places you in that office, were it even for a minute, you become responsible for it. The Superior puts you at the door: I must be careful to do it well, as if I had always been there. Today obedience sets me to knitting stockings, tomorrow to making bowls [?]: I must do it with the same diligence. Likewise the infirmarians must give the Superior an exact report, because the Superior is not at the sick person’s side and cannot know except from the report you give her. If you do so, you will do your duty and gain merits for yourself. For charity’s sake, sisters, if it is not a feast day, do not leave the sick person who is in a bad way in order to go and hear Mass; and with what heart will you approach Communion after having abandoned Jesus sick, who had need of you? What will He say to you? You let Me suffer and you come to receive Me? If it is a feast day, one has the Superior informed so that she may send two other sisters to relieve you. There are Masses also late, and the superior will send someone to relieve you, and then indeed you will be able to say to Jesus: Jesus, I have suffered for You all night, I have brought You a soul in Your arms, and now I come to receive the reward, receiving You into my breast. You see, if there are brutish men who will hear nothing of religion, do not speak to them of it; many times it is worth more to make them perform an act of resignation by making them laugh. Cheer him up and you will see that little by little he will come back, and you will do with him what you wish. I hope that you will do well, and that the air of Sampierdarena will not make you fall short in your vocation, and that you will do everything on your part to make this branch of our institute progress.

Let us now have the conference. On what shall we give it? We shall give it on obedience, of which we have such need.

Obedience is holy; obedience, the saints have said, is the surest road to make us saints, to lead us to the summit of Carmel. Obedience is that road which leads to the glory of Paradise without making us undergo the pains of Purgatory. There are three ways of reaching it. At the top of one is written: Humility, meekness, obedience; strip yourself of everything and I will lead you to Paradise; and this one is all full of thorns. The other is in flower; various roses are there, but some stones and thorns; however, little streams refresh the ground, and at the top of this one is written: poverty, humility, meekness, abasement of oneself. The third, then, is beautiful, broad, without stones; at its top it is in flower with roses, these too have their thorns, but gentle ones, and on it is written: this is the road that the lukewarm Virgins run, who do not want to feel themselves pricked too much. And why do we see that Virgin who turns back, and why? She ought to have embraced that thorn, that plant, and in fear she drew back. And so are you; that plant is the Superior who commands you, and you must obey without at all asking why; so she crosses the thorn-thicket, obeys cheerful and ready, and finds herself at the gate of paradise. I have spoken to you of the ordinary way, because the extraordinary one, unfortunately, you do not know; it is full of briars, thorns, hedges, annihilations, humiliations, denials of the will of every kind. Let us go to the ordinary one, which even young women who want to live well in the world have chosen; and shall a bride of the Lord not travel it? And without effort. Those plants that you will find on the road are the little mortifications that the Superior gives you. But you will say to me: she is a Superior who ill-treats me, and wrongly. I will answer you: Who is your Master? What did He do in the praetorium of Pilate, while they mocked Him, jeered at Him, insulted Him? He, all humble, suffered everything and presented all His humiliations to the Eternal Father in atonement for our sins.

Yes, my God, You have suffered so much, and shall I, a worm of this earth, not be able to humble myself and take the penance that will be imposed on me? The Superior calls me and says to me: I want to hear your justification. That one will answer at once. If the Superior does not want to hear me, well then, the Lord will justify me Himself; and she remains quiet and at peace. Eh! For the Lord left a St. Francis de Sales humiliated for so many years by a calumny pinned on him, and will He not permit us to be so in little things?

Yes, let it be: if we are not justified in this way, the Lord will justify us in Paradise. Someone will say: but I shall pass before my sisters for a wicked woman, for the most infamous of all. Blessed are you if it is so, because it will be a proof that you are a chosen soul of the Lord; you are dear to God. He wants to test your faithfulness and give you more glory in Paradise; and if you know how to cross this step, to take this rose, you will be blessed in Paradise. See how beautiful this road is. A saint used to say: obedience, obedience, how beautiful you are, how sublime you are. So let us love this virtue; let us obey without asking why. Yes, how beautiful this virtue is, how delightful is the way of Carmel, which without briars, without thorns, leads us to glory, to the blessed Eternity of Paradise.

How precious the vocation is, how necessary it is to thank the Lord for having given us so great a grace, how watchful we must be to preserve it and to drive away the temptations and doubts that may come to us about our State.

Every day we must say to ourselves: Where are you, O creature? And how much you owe to God for having given you such a grace; and you must think of advancing every day more and more in virtue. Dear daughters! Let us cast a glance at the past, when God came knocking at our heart, how many times, with impulses, with most lively inspirations, that we might correspond to the vocation; we consented, saying to God: Lord, here is Your Samuel. Every day God comes knocking at our heart, exhorting you to put your rules into practice; and indeed, when you come to depart from some rule, you are no longer at peace, because of those impulses that every day He made felt in your heart, some through charity towards the sick, towards the little girls; this you cannot deny. But alas, there comes the temptation of that diabolical spirit which comes into our heart, to some through the flesh and at times through the Spirit; it comes and says to her: See, if you had stayed in the World you would have done more good, in homes, in Churches, by teaching Catechism; in the world everyone would have called you the Saint; instead you came here with so many rules to observe; you have so many vows, of the sick [?]: will you be able to take them all upon yourself? In the world you could make the vows without the burden of so many rules; so they are so many sins if you fail in them. Here the flesh is not mortified but put to death. It whispers in the spirit: see, it says to you, you no longer enjoy the delights of your Bridegroom; do you know for certain that your vocation is here? These, we know, are true whisperings of the devil; we must answer with firmness, as the Martyrs, the Apostles answered. What did they answer? We have not come here to enjoy ourselves, while our master had nothing but thorns, nothing but tribulations. The Lord has said: whoever wants to come with Me, let him leave everything, father, mother, brothers, sisters, but let him take up his Cross and follow Me.

So we must think that we are not in the House of the Lord to have sweetness, consolations, but sorrows and death to ourselves. One is crucified in the flesh, another in the spirit; there are so many sorts of crucifixion. On Tabor no one can stay. The Lord made us go up Tabor when He made us hear His voice, gave us the Vocation; but we know well that the Lord did not stay on Tabor with His Apostles. So let us be jealous of it, let us guard this treasure, let us make it bear fruit, so that one day, the more fruit we have made it bear, the greater will be our glory. On that day we shall lay this fruit in the hands of our Jesus: behold, You gave me a treasure, I have made it bear fruit, and You give me that for which we have laboured. Every day let us seek to make it bear fruit. Ah! blessed will be that daughter of Saint Anne who will say: every day I have sought to advance in obedience, like Bl. Berchmans; every day I have sought to put into practice that word of my Superiors. We must never, however, become anxious if we fall again, because it is enough that I did it inadvertently; I have sought to be able to overcome myself in everything, and in particular in self-love, saying among yourselves: I see that every day I do all I can to begin. Believe that so great is the pleasure we give to the Heart of our Jesus when we begin to overcome ourselves and to labour, even in little things; believe that He takes note of everything and abounds in graces. So why do we not seek to give Him pleasure for so little? So why, if the Lord is content with so little and takes account of everything, why not make much of this vocation? Go back to that moment when He gave you the vocation, on that day when you presented yourselves in the parlour: if you had been told, you must take the discipline to the point of blood, everything would have seemed little to you and you would have let yourselves be cut to pieces; yes, because in that moment He had carried me onto Tabor. So why do we forget everything so quickly, become so quickly, so quickly weak? For charity’s sake, do not forget that moment; and your heart, once so lively, why let it now fall asleep? Ah! no, let us not put it in the tomb, which is that of the death of every good desire. For charity’s sake: if I had to describe to you the preciousness of this treasure, I would never finish; but I will tell you that when this ugly spirit comes to tempt us, let us answer it: away, for now is not the time; let us put everything under our feet; did we not come here for the Lord? To give death to our body? And when we receive offences, let us cast a glance at the Crucifix, let us think of His sufferings, for then ours will seem small, a nothing; and let us not run at once to complain of it in Church; is there not need of a somewhat nobler spirit, as Jesus has made us noble? We must be above all things, we must overcome everything that presents itself to us of humiliation: this is the first; the second, then, is to have esteem and veneration for our habit. I believe myself more than all the Queens of this earth, not because we should be held so, but because we are the brides of our Jesus, and one day this habit will have to make us shine in the presence of God; and if we want one day to be clothed with gems and precious pearls, then here below we must make much of this black habit, which one day up there will be changed into a white habit, as it was given to a good soul to see a daughter of Saint Anne dressed in white like a lily; the form of the habit was the same, but white, no longer black; it shone greatly.

And why such glory? Because she venerated this black habit, she grew in virtue and in her vocation. Do not do penances, but seek every day to advance in virtue, and one day you too will go to bless this habit and to enjoy the glory of Holy Paradise.

— 28 April 1872, given at Ferrara

how much self-love harms the soul

Ugly love [?], which aspires to nothing but comforts, to the goods of fortune — people of the world; religious, who cannot attend to these goods, it drives, alas, to make themselves seen and to appear better than the others, to hide their own defects, to suffer at being corrected, etc…

Self-love is bound up with all our faculties and puffs us up and submerges us. Many times self-love leads us not to want to make mistakes so that people will not speak ill of us. What has it done? It has won, making us fall into dejection, casting us down still more. If one could paint it with a brush, we would see it all branched out in our intellect. The creature who does everything with that thought, in order to make herself honoured, what becomes of her? She becomes fearful; she no longer does anything, for fear that her work may come under judgement and she will no longer have the praises she craves. But the Saints who aspired to perfection did not do so. They instead sought to be derided, mocked, humbled, and in their humiliations they rejoiced, because they resembled our Lord more. What is man, to be praised by another man? Ah! yes, for my part I will repeat: a day lost, that day on which I was praised; for me it has no currency; I want it from God. From God alone have we to receive our pay. And who ever sustains us in so many adversities? Having given pleasure to God. And who ever is that creature who can puff herself up by saying: today I was praised? A soul that loves God cannot have such thoughts; and in the evening, at the examen, what sorrow to think: today I was paid with a coin that has no substance. Oh! Yes, you see, I have seen persons puffed up with self-love, and then seen them in an instant cast down, humbled; and I said then: what is man without God, what are earthly praises! Ah! yes, let us leave all this, and we, as daughters of Saint Anne, the last born in the Church, let us say: we are in our misery; our Institute was born in sufferings, in desolation, but the stronger is its foundation. It was born in a ship that totters on all sides, beaten by the waves; but it will be sustained by the Lord, who, having tried it and tried it again, will lead it to the harbour of salvation. Let us say to Jesus: Yes, carry us on the wings of Your providence, to lead us then to the glory of Holy Paradise.

On the way in which we must bear with one another

Before beginning the Conference I will touch on some failings that I seem to have observed in these days.

The infirmarians, when they come home, do they give the report? How did they conduct themselves at the sick person’s? First one must give it, then the other; and woe if one should suspect that the other had told some fault of hers: she would fail in an important point of rule and would be lacking in virtue.

What have we come to do in this house? And how much we ought to thank the one who gives us occasion to make us know our defects and amend them; so, as of the Confessor, we may not speak of it; why, for so frivolous a pleasure, displease God? Tell me, do you not feel reluctance (?) while it is a thing so openly (…. illegible word)

I, you see, have always blessed my Superiors for having made me know my failings, my defects, because, you see, by ourselves we never know what they are. So too being calumniated: you see, our actions are never perfected except when we are opposed in our inclinations, because these make us take giant strides in the way of perfection.

So it ought to be with you: to be glad when you are corrected by your Superiors for some defect. We must not let this little boat of our Institute perish, which is now among the waves but which I hope will spread throughout the whole world. At the homes of the sick we must keep silence well, keep this tongue in check; one can cause those who listen to us to form thoughts that are not upright. Instead of talking, we ought at that time to make a spiritual Communion, which would be of benefit to your soul. Why do you stop at so frivolous a gratification? Which, once ended, is nothing but an insipid sip, nothing but a puff of wind that, having vanished, leaves in the one who listened to you nothing but suspicions about that Religious or person of whom she heard speak. Oh! The tongue, to say that it is the noblest part of the creature, and if one does not know how to use it for good, we see how much harm it can do. Let us see how the Saints knew how to keep it in check and to use it for good. We see it in a St. Anthony of Padua, whose tongue has been preserved intact for so many centuries; but why? Because he always used it to convert souls and to preach the Religion of Christ. We see, instead, to how many torments the tongue of those who used it to offend God has been reduced to suffer.

I will touch also a little on poverty, of which you also have need. Thanks be to God we are here where we lack nothing; but who has given us these things? Our Jesus has provided us with everything; but not for that must we waste things and say: oh! In the cellar there are so many; no, we must not say this, but rather say: these things belong to the Lord and we are obliged to preserve them. So take good care of the things entrusted to us; you see, in all the Monasteries, you see, they take care, they preserve even half a sheet of paper. One must take care to acquire the bearing of a religious, because what matters is not wearing the habit, but one must know how to put into practice the duties of a Religious.

We shall now say something on the way in which we must bear with one another, since, when we hear a somewhat sharp word said to us by a sister, there we are at once all fire, irritated towards her. Oh sisters, let us cast a glance at our Jesus: how much ill-treatment He suffered for us, and I may say how much He suffers now continually, and we make Him suffer by our listlessness and irreverence in Church; and we cannot tolerate a word not quite courteous from a sister. And shall we not be able to find a word to comfort another whom we see afflicted? Oh! Then is the moment to put into practice the beautiful virtue of Charity, of compassion one towards the other. What good is it in the morning to make resolutions on what we most fail in, and then when the occasion comes we do not know how to put them into practice? Those harsh words to one another, those rudenesses: do they denote love? Ah! no; and what would you do if the moment came to bear big ones, if now you cannot bear a single word said in one way rather than another? For example: a sister gives me a slap, offer her the other cheek; she speaks to me brusquely, you answer her with charity without even taking notice; one sees a sister afflicted, take care to console her, to comfort her: this is how the daughters of Saint Anne ought to be among themselves. Still more: a sister is tiresome; let us take care to comfort her and not give her occasion ourselves; sometimes it may be a physical ailment; what do we know? Another commits a fault: if it is such as must be told, let us tell it to the Superior without anyone noticing, so that she may remedy it; she will know how to admonish her; if it is small, let us keep silent about it, or else with a good word let us make it known to her; then indeed peace will reign in our house. We see a sister who is sad: let us comfort her; sometimes she may have something, dryness of spirit, something that torments her. Doing so, if she sees that Jesus dwells in our heart, that Jesus whom you receive every morning will be seen to be master in you. We have a patched veil, something is taken from us: let us keep silent, let us bear it with patience, for then we shall cross that road of peace which will lead us to Paradise.

on various points of our Holy Rules

I shall speak today about various faults which I have observed in you, which have greatly afflicted me, and which, before warning you of them, I wished to be quite certain of. A sister must not repeat to another what she has heard said of her either by the Superior or by the others, for what does she do? She does nothing but irritate the sister into failing in charity. I ask: what pleasure have you procured in reporting this to the sister? Perhaps she has an irascible spirit that would like to do everything well and to be praised, and to hear it reported that she has erred irritates her and makes her murmur; behold the harm the first sister does by having reported it to her. You see, I do not think myself good for anything; you have not learnt it from me; the religious who are around me can say that I do not do a thing without first asking their opinion, because many times they may know something that I do not know. And who is it that thinks herself irreproachable and claims never to do wrong, and would never wish to err so as not to be reproved?

Ah! this is subtle pride; and if by chance the Superior reproves her, there she is sulking. Ah! pride! No, she must humble herself, cast herself at her feet saying: yes, I have erred, tomorrow I shall do better. So too, a Sister finds something to say to her, and there she is at once sulking towards her; she does not speak to her, she no longer looks at her. Ah! Sisters, if we wish to live as good Christians, we must absolutely observe this point: to keep our will under the heel of the Superior, and likewise to keep our tongue in its place, because there can be no true peace if silence is not observed. If this beautiful point of the Rule, silence, is observed, there will be charity; there will be a hundred hearts in one heart alone. For if that sister, let us suppose, should burst out [?], the other at once answers her: yes, you are right, it is not right, the Superior scolds you wrongly. What sort of good sister does this one seem to you? Instead a true daughter of Saint Anne calms her, breaks off the conversation by keeping silent, or else with good manners makes her see the harm she does by speaking in such a way. For otherwise what happens? That one loses Communion, because after having said: what a Superior, it is not right, she is always reproving me, I cannot bear it any more, behold, she has murmured against her, against the Superior, and she will certainly no longer approach Communion. You see, Sisters, and do you believe that Superiors are without faults? The saints have fallen, and shall we not fall? I, who am not in the number of the saints, see that I must be well on my guard so as not to fall. Ah! Let us ask God for humility; there is no other way to amend ourselves than every morning to see in which things we fall most, to set them before our eyes and to make resolutions to amend ourselves of them. I cannot bear to hear one who says: I cannot overcome myself. Ah! yes, this is an expression hardly pleasant to hear pronounced by a daughter of Saint Anne. You will not be able to, it is true, of yourself, but ask it of God, for with His help you will have everything. He stands waiting for us with open arms, and seeks almost nothing else, nor desires anything else, than to communicate His graces to us. That is why we complain, saying: I do not receive a grace, I never grow in virtue. But tell me, just look, how have you prayed? You will have mumbled great Paters with a distracted mind; think a little whether you have united yourself with words of the heart to the Heart of God, in order to draw His Spirit from it. Eh! You see, I have seen so many little pious women who said Paters and knew nothing else but staying in Church, and then, as soon as they were outside the Church, at the first contrariety that befell them, there they were in a rage, bursting out [?] as never before; whereas those poor women who work all day, and in the evening, tired as can be from their toil, there they are at the foot of the Altar offering their labours to the Lord; yes, they know how to draw from that most sacred Heart the graces they need, in those moments of prayer and of union with their God. And we, on this day, while that Priest explained to us so well this solemnity of Pentecost, why were we too not set on fire by a spark of that blessed fire of which he spoke to us? Could not we, perhaps, have enjoyed that fire which enriched the Apostles with so many gifts of Knowledge, of wisdom? So that they no longer knew how to relish anything but God? And instead we have always remained with the same carnal senses of ours, whereas those of the Apostles became mortified [?], so that they lived on nothing any more but God alone? And why? Because we do not know how to unite ourselves and with fervent prayer to pray this divine fire to descend into our heart; and let us say to it that it may descend now and purge it of every vice, of every human affection. Oh! Yes, the Spirit of God is a most pure Spirit which enters a house that it finds empty of itself, and not into one who does not know how to strip herself of all that she remains surrounded by; and so long as we have not emptied ourselves of everything, of our own will, we shall never be able to receive the Spirit of God. Ah! how many times have I heard it said: he is a saint who before was a great sinner, and in a moment he was seized and filled with this divine fire; he emptied his heart of everything that savoured of the human; and so it would do with us if it found our heart empty of earthly affections.

We shall now pass on to some points of the Rule in which I have seen there is failing, as I said at the beginning. Obedience, as I have told you so many times, the daughters of Saint Anne have written upon their shoulders; this word obedience, instead, is carried on one shoulder only, so that with one we obey and with the other we transgress. The Superior commands me a thing; this is how one obeys: yes, I shall finish this and then I shall do it; the Superior has not commanded it to me, and I do not do it; instead of interpreting the desire of the Superior, that is what is said. So too, many times the Wardrobe-keeper gives us something: ah! this is not mine. This word “mine” must no longer be heard, because we are in Religion and everything is in common. I am given an item numbered for another, or else one stocking long and the other short; if we wish to go on to perfection we must keep them and not speak. And what will the Lord say to us on the day of Judgement? Ah! you could not wear a pair of tight stockings because they hurt your feet; ah! take a look at Mine, how you will find them pierced, and how they dripped blood as I went up to Calvary. And how do we wish to become saints if we do not wish to live the common life? A Blessed Bergmans became a saint by doing nothing other than the common life, because, you see, it is a true martyrdom to have to depend in everything, to have no will of one’s own. So too at dinner, how it pains me to hear it said: this is salty, this is tasteless. Try eating it for one day and then you will see that the second time it will no longer seem so bad to you. Do this: today I eat this thing that is bad for the conversion of poor sinners, another thing to obtain a grace that you desire, and then little by little everything will seem good to us. Let us do as the ant does, which goes about all day to find crumbs and hide them in its den for the winter, when, it raining, it cannot go out; let us take everything and set it aside for Eternity, for at the bed of death those mortifications which we shall have made in life will be a consolation to us. That good religious on her deathbed turns this way and that and sees those years in which she obeyed, those submissions which will make death sweet for her. I have always seen that those who seek a comfortable life struggle at death, not with death itself but with the humility [?] which they took pains in life to indulge in all its desires. Yes, dear daughters, let us take care, we to whom God has given so many lights, to profit by them and to make ourselves a great store of virtues and merits for Eternity. Let us try to observe Silence; there can be no peace and true spirit in our Houses if we do not observe Silence. Let us be submissive to the Superior even if, let us suppose, she is cantankerous; we must hold her as God; we must draw fruit from the reproofs she gives us, amending ourselves of our faults, even from calumnies, whether they come to you from the world. I have always seen that everything is the permission of God. I hear that they say something about me; I must always observe that I have something to amend or to improve in my actions. My sister makes known a fault of mine; I see at once to amend myself of it. Then yes, if we do so, we shall run the way of perfection and of the Saints.

Piacenza on poverty

I shall insist today on the point of Poverty, because this point will never be sufficiently explained and put into practice.

You know, O Sisters, that to go to Paradise one must be poor. This vow is contrary to our human nature, but it pleases our Lord so much that He chose it for His inheritance; He willed to be born poor, of a poor virgin, in a stable where there was nothing but a little straw. We are poor, but let us see how far we are from that Stable of Bethlehem. Let us see how much we neglect this Vow. The wardrobe-keeper in wasting things, in taking no care of the cotton, etc. The infirmarian in not taking care of and keeping in order the cloths of the sick, in not seeing to it that they are not lost; so too the cook. A day will come when our Guardian Angel will render account to God of all the failings in poverty that we have committed. We have left the world and consequently everything; and what does it matter that we toil at the bedside of the sick, that the teachers wear out their lungs with the girls, if then, for a worthless cloth wasted, we must lose the crown that is prepared for us? You will say to me: Mother knows nothing but to speak to us of this, we are poor enough. Oh my sisters, a Saint Teresa insisted on this point, and they were poorer than we; they eat lenten fare continually, they sleep on boards; and we have our bed, our rooms, we do not have the woollen shirt as they do. We, thanks be to God, lack nothing; we have chairs in Church to sit on; and what more do we desire? The Vow of Poverty may detach you from everything, but it does not detach you from keeping things in order. For example, I go into the garden, I see things on the ground, and one does not even deign to stoop and pick them up. Come now, I hope you will put this Vow into practice; especially to those who fail in it I leave this as an examen for the whole month; so too to those who fail in silence I leave silence as an examen; to those who fail in obedience I leave obedience. Now I wish to remove from you an apprehension that has arisen in some of you, namely that as soon as you are ill you will be sent away. Ah! no; of this you have had proofs, whether they are kept and whether they are cared for with assiduity and charity. You see, the sick are dearer to me, because, as we know, they have been visited by the Lord with an infirmity; but oh, it is for quite other things that they are sent away; certainly the Superiors must not tell the reason.

I shall tell you something about Charity, but it seems to me almost useless, because what must I say to persons who live together and who consequently must love one another, bear with one another, have compassion on the sick? You see, I love them all equally; if one falls ill, it is as though they took out one of my eyes; whether she be poor or rich, you see, I feel that I love them all equally; whether I go into one House or into another, I see them all with the eye of charity, as images of their Holy Mother. And how is it possible to be together and not love one another? And perhaps because she is old I should not have compassion on her? Ah! Yes, even more than a young one, because she is weaker and has more need of help.

Tomorrow is the Most Holy Trinity, a feast day beloved by me, for which I have always had devotion since I was a little girl. Tomorrow let us honour all Paradise, the Most Holy Triad, for which reason tomorrow will be a day of prayer. Yes, tomorrow, a beautiful day, a day of graces, a day on which the Most Holy Trinity holds its arms open to give us graces. We must therefore ask for graces, first for ourselves, that it may give us strength to persevere in our vocation until the end of our days, and then for the Institute, that it may send us a little providence; not because we are without it, but because we have to do certain small works, and if we had more providence we could open the door to so many poor postulants who stand at the door anxious to enter, among whom who knows how many there will be into whom God will have infused His Spirit and called here to become saints.

Let us now pass to ourselves; let us begin to take a look from the very morning and see whether our heart begins to be stripped of that veil which prevents it from loving God, that God who in the morning comes into our heart to transform it in such a way that it no longer knows what earth is. So then, in the morning, that voice which wakes us and makes itself heard in our ear is the voice of the Holy Mother, so that our heart can no longer live under the blankets and flies to that Being by whom it is wholly possessed, and betakes itself to His feet; there it hears the point of the Meditation, that point which every morning comes to rouse us. So then, that heart all aflame with divine love, how can it fall asleep while it is in the presence of its Beloved? And while it meditates on His passion? The further it goes on in meditation, the more it is kindled with divine love; that heart is already wholly in Paradise, it no longer feels earthly love; we possess everything; having God with us we have all the kingdoms of earth and of Heaven. Let us go further: those sweet words of the Litanies rouse us and loosen [?] for us, one by one, the sweet words of Jesus; at every instant that repeating of the sweet name of Jesus, which seems to say to us: prepare yourself, for soon I shall come into you. Ah! If we considered what Communion is! If we often do not feel consolations, it is that we do not prepare ourselves as we ought to receive Jesus; many times, then, it is through aridity. God left Saint Catherine of Siena in it for a long time; but well, let us leave this subject to the confessors, to those who guide us, and let us go on to that sweet feeling which God communicates to those who love Him. A Saint Philip Neri said: Ah! Lord, withdraw from me, for You make me die. You will say to me: but he was a Saint. Yes, I shall answer you, the Lord wants you all to be saints. You must not think of vague things of no importance, about the house, about some word overheard that may disturb you. Ah! yes, that Religious who goes about to listen, to find out, what will she be able to feel in Communion, in Meditation? Yes, the devil has much to toil over in this work, because it is a work of God, and he must suffer at seeing the mission that we have. You see, at Ferrara we have more than 140 girls, all taken out of sin; so it is no wonder if this work is assailed. Never in the world has a work been seen to flourish so quickly as this one; every day there are new crosses; but I keep saying: these are the foundations that make the walls of our House, of our Institute, more solid; I am not dismayed, rather I rejoice at it. Ah! Yes, dear daughters, you are in a sea of milk; you do not hear the noises, the crimes of the world in these times, in which the chastisement must be near. Ah! how much you must thank God for having led you here and gathered you within His walls, in the work of Saint Anne, which can never collapse and will last eternally for all ages of ages, amen.

given at Ferrara on 1 June 1872

On the charity which the Daughters of Saint Anne must have among themselves

What I have observed with sorrow is that Charity is not observed in all our poor Houses as I should desire; therefore today I shall speak to you on this point, since we, more than any other Religious, must practise this virtue today, finding ourselves always in occasions where we must exercise it. If we wish to have charity towards those outside, we must first of all exercise it towards ourselves, one with another, bearing with one another, contenting everyone, relieving whichever of us we see afflicted. We must see to it that the end of every action of ours is God and not our own satisfaction; we must try to be ready and vigilant, to occupy the lowest places; those actions which God gives us the grace to see abhorred by men, the more beautiful they will be in the eyes of God. Look purely to the glory of God alone, and set this as the foundation of every action of ours. The Saints knew that by that humiliation they gave pleasure to God; at once they embraced it, because they knew that they gave pleasure and glory to God.

The mortification of ourselves gives pleasure to God; we must mortify our interior and exterior senses. Let us take the exterior ones, which are: abstaining from eating, from drinking, from eating things pleasing to our palate, not eating outside mealtimes, subjecting our body to the rigours of the seasons; assisting the sick, for all the Saints have had to pass along this road. A Saint Rose of Lima, who, while with a sick person, sees a cup of blood and feels herself shudder and her stomach turn; then what does she do? She takes the cup and drinks it. I go, for example, into the kitchen, I see a piece of bread, the desire comes to me to take it; yielding to the senses, I take it and put it in my mouth; at that moment a girl or a sister passes by, sees her and takes scandal from it; thus this one has done two wrongs, one for not having known how to mortify herself, the other for the scandal she has given. So too, mortify yourselves even in the ordinary things of eating, and say: Lord, I make You an offering of it; and do as the saints, who found occasion to mortify themselves in everything; it was precisely these abstinences that brought them to union with God, to those perfect unions which united their soul to God. So too, mortify yourselves in words, observing silence. For example: I come out of the parlour, I do not know that it is silence, I speak; this is not wrong, provided that, once aware that it is the hour of silence, I correct myself by keeping silent; because if instead I knew that it was silence and I spoke, it would be a great imperfection that I should commit. These small imperfections, I assure you, are those which will (not) make you saints.

We have then the third point, which is our consideration of ourselves. What are we? A handful of dust. The more God grants us graces, the more we know what we are and humble ourselves, if these graces are true and come to us truly from God. For example: God grants us today a great grace, He makes us know the immensity of His greatness, so that the creature humbles herself, makes herself a toad, knows herself to be the most abject creature on this earth; and this way of acting of hers is what makes her pleasing before God; and if she had to make a million humiliations before everyone, she goes to meet them joyfully, because she holds that she has a great hunger [?] for them, and in this way they are truly safe; whereas when they are praised they fear falling into pride, losing God, because they know that if God withdraws from them they are nothing, they no longer do anything good; and it is for this reason that they so distrust themselves.

I have observed, you see, that those Religious full of self-love, wishing to appear more than they do — you see, I have frequented some religious, those full of self-love, of the esteem of others — in all the works, the embroideries they made and for which they believed they would have praise, the Lord, in order to humble them, made them appear, when they were presented, full of mistakes and badly executed. Whereas, you see, that humble person, God seeks to raise her up. You see, at Genova, a most humble person was commanded to do a work in gold which she had never done; she did it out of obedience, she carried it out, and when it was presented it was seen by priests and by persons of talent, and it was most beautiful and well executed. God did this to reward her humility, and so will He do to us. I could tell so many facts that I should never finish, but I shall only tell you that it is the truth of the Gospel that whoever humbles himself shall be exalted and whoever exalts himself shall be humbled.

given at Piacenza on various points of the Rules

I have many things to tell you today; I begin to speak of [?] our dear Mother, but first we shall speak of the Church, in which each one must stay in the place assigned to her by the Superior, and not put herself in one pew today and in another tomorrow, that is, take the place of others; likewise not to take the books of this one and that one and never bring them back to their place. But this would still be the least; the greater thing is that one fails in a Rule which says: you shall not take the things of another without permission. And likewise not to lay your head on the books, because they get dirty; besides being unbecoming, one fails in poverty. Do you wish to lean your forehead? Lean it on your hands, on your handkerchief, but never on the books. Tell me a little: on feast days, after the reading, I saw that you go into the garden, scattered here and there, instead of going to Church, since Sunday is consecrated to God, and so taking that free moment which one cannot have during the whole week. So too in the morning, all be ready for Meditation, because this is the first point of a Religious; whoever does not meditate is not sure of eternal life and cannot ascend to perfection. So too at the midday prayers, all be present; and when the bell rings for the Angelus Domini, those at the looms must come at once to the chapel to recite it. It is two days since I warned you, and it goes well; why could you not always do it?

Try, when the bell rings for prayers, to run promptly to the voice of the Lord who calls us; try to be the first, otherwise, when we are in the presence of the Lord, we shall be severely judged in this too. And if for some reason one cannot be at prayers, one makes one’s excuses to the Superior, telling her why; but do not make it a habit not to go, saying: Oh! the Superior knows it; I shall finish this, so then I shall find it done; I shall say the prayers by myself. Very well, but do you not know that saying them alone you will not be able to say them as well as in community? And then in the evening examen you will find yourself confused, not knowing whether we have truly failed out of necessity or out of negligence, and then, behold, a point of the Rules has been broken. So too the reading, the last point of the rule of the day: I have seen that it is neglected, it is done with indolence, people ask to go to bed. And do you not know that you fail in an essential point of your Rules? For reading is the food of the soul, and no one has become a Saint without spiritual reading; and what good thoughts can that religious have going to bed, if she does not end the day with spiritual reading? I, you see, if I do not do it with you, being at the door or for some necessity, do it in my room by myself; and so, you see, in the night I always dream either that I am in Church, or that I am making my Communion, or that I am receiving the blessing. For, you see, if one does not fall asleep with some good thought or making a spiritual Communion, one may easily have bad dreams.

We shall now pass to the conversations held among you, which lead not only to failings in charity but also to murmuring; and it is true that without spiritual reading one can neither have good thoughts nor hold good conversations. And so one forms suspicions of one another, of what the Superiors do, and untrue things are reported. You see, although every day I see the muddy water of the fountain flowing, I see faults, yet I always say within myself: she will not have done it with malice, she will have done it inadvertently, and I cannot think ill of it, unless I see a failing against the Rule. For example: I see the infirmarian who has not done her office well for me; well then, without thinking further, I know that there is the Superior who will see to correcting her. Indeed, you see, it is idleness that makes one form suspicions, saying: O sisters, it is not going well at the Casa del Verme, they do this, the Superior there, the Mother has said this — all untrue things, because they have heard badly and so reported it worse, and added other things. What does it do? Whatever becomes of that poor sister? She is beside herself on hearing this, she does not know what has become of her in the eyes of the Superiors; and so what does she do? She murmurs against the superiors, she loses her peace; and the other who has spoken ill does not know what to do, she grows languid; to make her Communion or not to make it is all the same, and it comes about that she gives up Communion altogether. But tell me: where is the charity that Jesus Christ teaches us, He who is all charity? We must imitate Him, never seeing faults in our fellow sisters, always thinking that if she has done wrong she has done it out of foolishness and not out of malice, as I think, and not going about making rash judgements; because to think that a Sister has done something wrong without knowing it for certain is a rash judgement, and this is worse than murmuring.

I recommend prayer to you; do it from the heart; I see that there is not much of it. Oh! a fine thing, you will say to me, you do not see into our heart. No, you are right; I have never said that I see into your consciences, but I see it from your behaviour, from your conversations: nothing else is spoken of but eating. This dish pleases me, it does not please me, it is good, it is bad; never of the things of God. Oh! how will our Jesus enter into you in the morning? Oh! I shall say that He will enter barely onto the tongue — I do not say into the breast, but not even into the heart; because then it would be impossible, with Jesus in the heart, to be able to think of keeping up this wretched body. I do not say that one must not eat one thing with more pleasure than another, because God does not call all to the same perfection, like the Curé of Ars, who fed on potatoes alone and on the food of the poor; but rather to nourish oneself so as to be able to work more, and not for pleasure. Although I am setting this out, I cannot believe it myself, because to think that in the House of Saint Anne such beings dwell would tear my soul, while having the finest career that can be given: that of the Saints.

I, on seeing that infirmarian whom God covers with the mantle of Charity — that if she has done her office well, at her death not only will she not undergo the pains of purgatory, but she will die the death of the Saints and will fly straight to Paradise. Yes, in truth, that infirmarian who does her office with charity, without self-love, it will not surprise me if she comes to work miracles; because, you see, I say that the person who practises charity without self-love will be able to share in the mercies of God; because, you see, if self-love enters into you it absorbs all your good actions. And let us suppose that one has nursed a woman with gangrene, one full of sores, has assisted her in her agony and even dressed her, and then tells of what she has done with vainglory: behold, the poor thing has lost everything, nothing remains to her. Whereas let us see another who has done less but with humility: before God that action of charity will be rewarded, and she will find herself rich in virtue and will have graces from God, like Saint Aloysius, who died a martyr of charity; because, you see, God crowns the end of the days of the infirmarian with martyrdom; and let her not say: see, I have caught this illness, see what one gains in here, and then I am not cared for. But you will say: but if I feel this, I cannot help it. It does not matter to feel, but to consent; indeed, you see, one who is more sensitive will feel more than another, but if she makes an effort she has more merit before God. A Saint Francis de Sales used to say: I should like my self-love to die a quarter of an hour before me. Returning to prayer, I should like it to be well done; and then you say: I am not heard. Ah! But why do you not pray well? You could be heard in a moment, in a day. You must pray with humility, because whoever prays without humility, with pride, God cannot hear; so let us root out of our heart the ugly monster of self-love. If, for example, we understand that this action may lead me to self-love, to honour, ah! then let us leave it; let everything go, so that we may not lose our soul.

Let the infirmarian, in her noble office at the bedside of the sick, be humble and free from thoughts of pride and vainglory. You see, the masters of the Spirit, in order to know whether a work is truly of God, look to see whether it appropriates nothing to itself; then indeed they know whether it is the true spirit of God.

In this month consecrated to Saint Anne, take this as your midday examen, and see whether self-love enters into any of your actions; pray to her and make resolutions to amend yourselves of it.

of the day 14 July 1872 given at Piacenza

On Various observations

First of all, I shall tell you a little of what I was thinking today. I was in that hovel of our room doing the cleaning; I thought to myself: will the nuns not also have their little room to clean? To sweep, to wash, etc., instead of wandering about the house. Religious who love cleanliness so much are Brides of the Lord and know that they must be clean. I imagine what it must be like in your room; the other day I saw one where the pigsty was much better than it. What you ought to say is: Oh, at this hour I shall go and do a little cleaning in our little room. You see, if one goes to the Dominican nuns, one sees behind the door of their room a broom and a dustpan [?]; do not think that they have a maid; they do everything themselves. I wish, therefore, that whenever you can you should clean it and wash it, make the bed well, remove the dust, cobwebs, etc.

If you do not have a broom, ask for one and it will be given to you. Listen: if I have done it, you too can do it; your little room is not even as large as mine; it seems smaller to me. So too those who are two together, so much the better: they help one another and do it more quickly; one does one thing, the other does another. On the contrary, what do you do on Sundays? You wander now about the house, now in the garden, thus staying idle. And by good fortune the Religious all go out during the day — the Lord knows why I send them to the sick — and in spite of this, those who remain wander about; one goes into the office of another to tell her what she has heard, and to see whether that one also knows something, and so on; doing so, it is difficult not to fall into murmuring. Now I shall tell you that I have thought of making a little timetable so that the sick need not fret, nor the infirmarian, nor the poor Cook; and this will send you what you are to have for food. You already know that when the Lord wishes to bring a soul to a higher degree He sends it infirmities, which, borne with patience, gain you a crown of glory in Paradise. So then, since infirmity is so precious a treasure, let us not waste it on such frivolous things, on trifles; instead of saying: today I have a headache, I should need coffee, ice; I did not eat at table, give me a biscuit, a sweet. Nonsense, all gluttony; so you wish to waste a grace that God gives you? I have seen so many Institutes, for example that of Saint Francis of Paola, whose friars eat plain lenten fare, all with oil; but when they are sick they have broth, they eat meat. But this Saint, so shrewd, said: Oh! I shall lay down a rule, so that they may not abuse it. So I too have thought of doing, although we are not so austere as they, since I see that your table is not so very meagre after all; and I should never have believed that one would come to so many softnesses as those of the young Ladies whom you go to assist. Oh! I should not then wish to have the scruple that a daughter of Saint Anne should have to pay for these gluttonies of hers, since after so much suffering as she has done here, I should not wish her to have to undergo a long purgatory there. So I have made this timetable, of which the infirmarian will keep one copy and the dispenser another, so that the sick sister will also have the benefit of living the common life even in her infirmities, and thus her glory will be greater; and I hope the house infirmarian will be content. I have also thought of putting together today. I have also thought of putting together today a little timetable for adoration too. Now I must speak of a point which I see you have not well understood, and it is of the first importance for you infirmarians, namely that with the sick you must never separate from each other. I shall explain to you why this point is so essential, and why there are very heavy penances for it, even that of being sent away; and you will see whether the one who laid this down was right. Except in the case where the infirmarians, giving the Superior an account of what there is in that house and why one must move away, the Superior, on the basis of the accounts she hears from her daughters, will say whether you may separate, yes or no.

Otherwise never. But see how beautiful this point is, of always going two by two: one is the Guardian Angel of the other. For, you see, for example, one goes alone into the other room, a manservant passes, comes up to her and says a little something to her; she, keeping her modesty, repels him. Then, behold, what does he do, irritated? He says: I shall make you pay for this; and so he says so many things about this poor sister, he has it put in the newspapers; she may well try to clear herself, she had no one as a witness. Whereas he could not say this if he had found them two together.

Let us suppose another will come and say: this Religious said this, did that; but the sister will be able to reply: but we have always been two, always together, we have never separated. In this way she will be able to save the sister, and so you are both saved.

Another case: for example, a thoughtless sister goes alone to light the way [?] for the Doctor, who at that hour happens to be drunk; he says an immodest word to her, makes a gesture at you, and then goes and says that the sister consented to it; and being alone she cannot clear herself; whereas being always two, always with the Guardian Angel at one’s side, this cannot happen. So you see how weighty this point is and with what scrupulousness you must observe it. So, for example, I am only going into the next room to see what time it is: I call the sister, my Guardian Angel, so that rascal cannot come and say: you handed me a note. So too, do not speak with the Doctor except out of necessity, to know in what way you are to give the medicines to the sick person, and nothing more. It is better that they say: they are Religious without a tongue, they have been brought up by that one… they must have orders not to speak. Let them say it; it is enough that before God we are innocent. So too there will be one who says: I am going alone, the sister is asleep, she does not see me and will not know. Ah! yes, it is a mercy if the sister does not wake; because today one thing will be said, tomorrow two, and not making a scruple of it one passes to laxity, and one speaks, one laughs, one tramples on a point of the rule.

When you come home, tell the Superior whether there has been talking, let the sister look to the one she had as companion, having said this on the way; and let her not keep silent for fear of falling into the bad graces of that sister who has affection for her, who is fond of her. She does not do well, because by keeping silent she may be the cause of that sister losing her vocation; whereas with one word said to the Superior, the latter makes her see her fault and she can amend herself.

With the prayers I am more content; you are all in the Chapel; there is not a day on which I do not count 15 or 16 of you, and I no longer find anyone wandering about, except one day when, going round the House, I found one, whom I shall call in due time. Yes, sisters, prayers made in common have more merit, and we shall not fear at the time of death that God may say to us: ah! you avoided Me, I avoid you too. Let those who arrive from outside quickly take off their veil; if they do not arrive earlier, let them at least say the Angelus Domini in common, and afterwards, in silence, all to table to take nourishment, not to please this body but for the spirit. You see, there is nothing else that brings peace; union in Communities will have the blessing of God, since, as you know, He said: “Whoever gathers several persons in My name, I shall be in their midst”

of the day 21 July 1872

Faults which the Mother corrected

Let us return today to cleanliness, of which I have spoken to you at other times, especially to the composure of one’s person. When we are before some person, you know well, I have told you, we must not do uncivil things. Well then, now I shall tell you of something that happened in one of our Houses, and after this a second that happened truly in this house not two days ago. In the first House a thoughtless sister was sent to a lady to keep the night watch; she pulled down her stockings, took off her shoes, for what reason I do not know. Well, this lady mortified her herself; she would no longer have her near her bed, and sent word to the Superior not to send her any more of them. Now something worse happens here among us: a sister lifted her skirts and looked for fleas on her legs, pulling down her stockings; and do you know what the sick woman said, complaining all night? They have brought me fleas, what have they brought me! They send word to me that we bring fleas; that is what I have to hear said to me; these are the consolations you give me. I have told you so many times: the sick may be dirty, full of vermin, but they want the infirmarians, the persons who care for them, to be clean. And yet, you see, this happened with old infirmarians, not with the new ones. I am not speaking to all, since there are good ones, and it is this that gives me a little strength and courage; one sees that the Lord has known how to keep them for Himself. Tell me a little: the other morning, when there was such a commotion over the veils, so that you scandalised the poor postulants and the sisters, you may be thankful that we are in the novena of the Holy Mother, otherwise I would have taken Communion away from all of you; but these being the eight days, I did not wish to embitter the Heart of the Holy Mother.

You ought, without a murmur, to have gone to the Superior; she would have given you another, or else, as a Mother, she would have made a search for it.

Now tell me a little: does it seem humility to you to undergo punishments, like that of the other day, grumbling, making yourselves ill? Look, you may be able to play that on a new Superior, of little experience, who is still naive, but not on me, because, you know, I weigh you all and I know what you all think. Do not believe that I know it from others or through revelations, for I have none; it is through experience. Yesterday too someone tried to play it on me, but she could not, and in due time I shall call her. So too, why take it out on this one or that one because she reported my fault to the Superior? Yes, I repeat it, and I tell you that the sister is obliged to report what she has seen of the other, and if she does not do so, she will bear all the harm that the other sister will have done. Both must have a hundred eyes, one for the other, and on returning Home tell the Superior everything that has happened. You who are always among the inns must be serious with everyone, old and young; look upon men as if they were wolves, flee from them. A manservant comes, brings a cup of water; the sister stays longer than needed, answering perhaps an idle word, and this is enough to give that wolf the opportunity, with cunning and other devices, to come and make you fall into the greatest of disorders. In short, you must be the guardian angel of each other, without ever separating; if you need something, ring — I command it of you — never separate, because you do not know what may happen in these places. I tremble when I see you go into the inns and into the houses of the nobility, because there is greater danger there than in the houses of the poor.
